Surah al-A'raf

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Alif. Lam. Mim. Sad.﴾ Al-Zajjaj said: The preferred interpretation of it is what Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: "I am Allah, the All-Knowing, and I make distinct" (ana Allahu a'lamu wa ufassilu).

﴿Kitābun﴾ (a book) is the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "it is a book."

﴿unzila ilayka﴾ (it has been sent down to you) is its description (ṣifah). What is meant by "the Book" is the surah.

﴿fa-lā yakun fī ṣadrika ḥarajun minhu﴾ (so let there not be any constraint in your breast about it): ḥarajun here means doubt, and doubt is called ḥaraj because the one who doubts has a constricted chest, just as the one who is certain has an expanded, open chest. The meaning is: there is no doubt that it is sent down from Allah. Or, ḥarajun minhu means (constraint) regarding its conveyance (tablīgh), because he feared his people, their denial of him, their turning away from him, and their harm to him, so his chest would constrict from the harm and he would not be eager to convey it. So Allah assured him and forbade him from concern for them. The prohibition is directed at the constraint, and there is much eloquence in it. The fā' (fa) is for conjunction (ʿaṭf), meaning: this Book I have sent down to you, so after its sending down let there be no constraint in your breast. 

The lām in ﴿li-tunḏira bihi﴾ (that you may warn with it) is connected to unzila, meaning: it was sent down to you for you to warn with it. Or it is connected to the prohibition, because if he is not made to fear, he will warn them; likewise, when he is certain that it is from Allah, certainty encourages him to warn with it, because the possessor of certainty is bold and relies upon his Lord.

﴿wa-dhikrā lil-mu'minīn﴾ (and a reminder for the believers) is in a position of naṣb (accusative) by an implied verb of its own, meaning: "that you may warn with it and remind with a reminder." So dhikrā is a noun with the meaning of reminding (tadhkīr). Or it is in the nominative (rafʿ) by coordination with kitābun, meaning: it is a book and a reminder for the believers. Or it is the predicate of an omitted subject (p-555), or it is in the genitive (jarr) by coordination with the position of li-tunḏira, meaning: for warning and for reminding.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 3:

﴿Follow what has been sent down to you from your Lord﴾, i.e., the Qur'an and the Sunnah,

﴿and do not follow other than Him﴾, other than Allah, "protectors" (awliya'), i.e., do not take as allies, apart from Him, the devils of the jinn and of mankind, who would lead you to the worship of idols, of desires (ahwa'), and of innovations (bid'ah).

﴿Little do you remember﴾, in that you abandon the religion of Allah and follow other than it. "Qalilan" (little) is in the accusative, governed by "tadhkurun" (you remember), i.e., you remember with little remembrance. And "ma" is superfluous (zā'idah), for emphasizing the smallness (of the remembrance), (tatadhakkarun) — Shami.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 4:

﴿وَكَمْ﴾ (wa-kam, "and how many") is the subject (mubtada'), ﴿مِن قَرْيَةٍ﴾ (min qaryah, "of a town") is a specifying element (tabyin), and the predicate (khabar) is ﴿أهْلَكْناها﴾ (ahlaknaha, "We destroyed it"), meaning: We intended its destruction, as in His saying: ﴿إذا قُمْتُمْ إلى الصَلاةِ﴾ ("When you rise up to prayer," Qur'an 5:6), ﴿فَجاءَها﴾ ("so there came upon it") meaning its people came, ﴿بَأْسُنا﴾ (ba'suna, "Our punishment") meaning Our chastisement, ﴿بَياتًا﴾ (bayatan, "by night") is a verbal noun (masdar) occupying the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), in the sense of "while they were spending the night" (ba'itin). It is said: baata bayatan hasanan (he spent the night in a good manner).

﴿أوْ هم قائِلُونَ﴾ ("or they were taking their midday rest") is a circumstantial clause conjoined (ma'tufah) to bayatan, as if it were said: "Our punishment came upon them while they were spending the night, or while they were taking their midday rest." The phrase is "hum qa'ilun" without a waw, and one does not say "jaaani Zayd huwa faris" without a waw, because when it was conjoined to a circumstantial clause before it, the waw was dropped to avoid the heaviness of two conjunctive particles together, since the waw of the circumstantial clause is the waw of conjunction, borrowed for linking. These two times were singled out because they are times of heedlessness, so the descent of punishment in them is more severe and more dreadful. The people of Lut (peace be upon him) were destroyed at night, at the time of dawn (sahar), and the people of Shu'ayb (peace be upon him) at the time of midday rest (qaylulah). It is also said: bayatan means "at night," i.e., at night while they were sleeping, or "by day" while they were taking their midday rest.

Qur'anic quotations are rendered as given. The passage is a short grammatical and exegetical note on 7:5.

﴿So their plea was not⦅ ... ⦆﴾ — their supplication and their humble entreaty (تَضَرُّع, tadarru').

﴿when Our punishment came upon them⦆ — when the first signs of the punishment came to them: ﴿except that they said, "Indeed, we were wrongdoers."⦆ They acknowledged the wrongdoing against themselves and the shirk (associating partners with God), at a time when that acknowledgment no longer benefited them. "Their plea" (دَعْواهُم) is the subject of kāna (كانَ, "was"), and "that they said" (أنْ قالُوا) is its predicate (خَبَر, khabar); the reverse is also permissible.

﴿So We will surely question those to whom messengers were sent﴾. "أُرْسِلَ" is predicated to "إلَيْهِمْ" (the verb "ursila," "was sent," has "ilayhim," "to them," as its deputy subject), meaning: (p-٥٥٦) "So We will surely question the one sent to them," and they are the nations, "about what they answered their messengers with." ﴿And We will surely question the messengers﴾ "about what answer they were given."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 7:

﴿So We will surely relate to them﴾ (to the messengers and to those to whom they were sent) what they did, ﴿with knowledge﴾, being knowers of their outward and inward states, their words, and their deeds.

﴿And We were not absent﴾ from them, nor from anything that proceeded from them. The meaning of the questioning (suʾal) is rebuke (tawbikh), reproach (taqriʻ), and confrontation (taqrir), when they speak with their tongues and their prophets bear witness against them.

﴿And the weighing﴾, i.e., the weighing of deeds and the distinguishing between their heavy and light, is a subject (mubtada'), and its predicate (khabar) is ﴿on that day﴾, i.e., the day when God questions the nations and their messengers. The clause was omitted, and tanwin (nunation) was substituted in its place. ﴿The truth﴾, i.e., justice, is its attribute. Then it was said: the scrolls of deeds will be weighed with a scale that has a tongue and two pans, to demonstrate the attribute and to cut off excuses. It was also said: it is an expression for the sound judgment and the just ruling, and God knows best its modality.

﴿Then whoever's scales are heavy﴾: mawazin is the plural of mizan or of mawzun, i.e., whoever's weighed deeds outweigh, which are those that have weight and measure, namely the good deeds, or that by which their good deeds are weighed. ﴿Those are the successful﴾, the winners.

﷿ "And as for those whose scales are light" — they are the disbelievers, for they have no faith, so that any deed could be weighed alongside it. Thus there is no good in their scale, and their scales are light. ﴿Those are the ones who have lost their souls because they used to wrong Our signs﴾ — they deny them. So the "signs" (āyāt) are the proofs (ḥujaj), and wronging them (al-ẓulm bihā) is placing them in other than their proper place, i.e., denying them and refusing to submit to them.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on surah 7, verse 10:

﴿And We have certainly established you on the earth﴾. That is, We made for you in it a place of settlement and a dwelling. Or it means: We established you in it and empowered you to dispose of it. ﴿And We made for you therein means of livelihood (*ma'ayish*)﴾. It is the plural of *ma'isha* (livelihood), which is what one lives by: food, drink, and other things. The correct form is to write the *ya'* explicitly (*tasrih al-ya'*, making the *ya'* clear), because it is original (*asliyya*), unlike in *sahaif* (pages), where the *ya'* is an added letter (*za'ida*). It is reported from Nafi' that he pronounced it with a *hamza*, by analogy (*tashbih*) with *sahaif* (p-557). ﴿Little is it that you give thanks﴾, like ﴿Little is it that you remember﴾ [al-A'raf: 3].

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 11:

﴿And We have certainly created you, then We have fashioned you﴾ means: We created your father Adam, peace be upon him, from clay without form, then We fashioned him after that. Its evidence is ﴿Then We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam," and they prostrated, except Iblis; he was not among those who prostrated﴾, meaning he was not among those who prostrated to Adam, peace be upon him.

**"Ma"** is in the nominative (raf'), meaning: what thing prevented you from prostrating? **"La"** is *za'idah* (superfluous, a particle with no semantic function here), as shown by the verse ﴿What prevented you from prostrating to what I created with My hands?﴾ (Sad, 38:75). A similar case is ﴿so that the People of the Book would know﴾ (al-Hadid, 57:29), where **"li-la"** means **"li"** (so that). ﴿When I commanded you﴾: in this there is evidence that the command indicates obligation (*wujub*), and the question about what prevented him from prostrating, despite his knowledge of it, is for rebuke, to show his opposition, his disbelief, his arrogance, his pride in his origin, and his contempt for the origin of Adam, peace be upon him.

﴿He said: "I am better than him. You created me from fire"﴾, and fire is a luminous substance (*jawhar nurani*), ﴿"and You created him from clay"﴾, and clay is a dark substance (*zulmani*). The wretch was mistaken. Rather, clay is superior because of its steadiness and dignity, and from it come forbearance, modesty and patience. That calls one to repentance and seeking forgiveness. In fire are frivolity, hot-temperedness and haughtiness, and that calls one to arrogance. Earth is the foundation of kingdoms, and fire is the foundation of destruction. Fire is a cause of betrayal and annihilation, and earth is a sign of trustworthiness and growth. Clay extinguishes fire and destroys it, while fire does not destroy it. These are virtues that Iblis overlooked, until he slipped into a corrupt form of reasoning. The statement of one who denies analogical reasoning (*qiyas*), "The first to practise analogy was Iblis," is itself an analogy, since analogy, according to its proponent, is rejected in the presence of a explicit text (*nass*). Iblis's analogy was a stubborn opposition to an explicit command.

The answer to "What prevented you?" should have been, "What prevented me was such-and-such." Instead he said, "I am better than him," because he had begun a new narrative, in which he spoke about himself, claiming superiority over Adam, peace be upon him, and gave the reason for that superiority. From this the answer is understood, as if he had said, "What prevented me from prostrating was my superiority over him," and in addition to this, he denied the command and considered it unlikely that one like himself should be commanded to prostrate to one like him, since the prostration of the superior to the inferior lies outside what is right.

(p. 558)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 13:

﴿He said: "Then descend from it"﴾ from the Garden, or from the heaven, because he was in it, and it is the place of the obedient and the humble. The fa' in "fahbit" (then descend) is a response to his saying: ﴿"I am better than him"﴾, meaning: if you are arrogant, then descend. ﴿So it is not for you﴾, meaning it is not proper for you ﴿to be arrogant therein﴾ and disobey, ﴿so go out, for you are among the debased﴾, those of abasement and humiliation before Allah and before His friends. Every person will blame you, and every tongue will curse you for your arrogance. And by this it is known that abasement is necessarily attached to arrogance (al-istikbar).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 14:

﴿He said, "Reprieve me until the day they are resurrected."﴾ "Reprieve me" means: grant me respite until the Day of Resurrection (al-ba'th), which is the time of the final blast (al-nafkhah al-akhirah) [of the Trumpet].

﴿He said: "Indeed you are among those given respite"﴾ until the first blast. This request was granted to him because of the trial it contains, and because it brings the hearts of those who love closer. That is, "This is My kindness toward one who wrongs Me; how much more toward one who loves Me?!" He emboldened him to ask, despite the lapse that had already come from him, because of his knowledge of the forbearance of the Lord of Majesty.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 16:

﴿He said: "Because You have led me astray"﴾ — i.e., misguided me. That is, "because of Your leading me astray," and the bā' (preposition "bi-") is connected to a suppressed verb of oath; its estimate is: "Because of Your leading me astray, I swear," or the bā' is for oath, meaning: "So I swear by Your leading me astray."

﴿Surely I shall sit in ambush for them on Your straight path﴾ — I shall block them on the path of Islam, lying in wait to turn them back and confronting them to bar them, just as an enemy lies in wait on the road to cut it off from travelers. Its accusative is adverbial of place (ẓarf), like your saying: "Zayd was struck the back," meaning: "on the back." It is related from Ṭāwūs that he was in the Sacred Mosque when a Qadarite man came, and Ṭāwūs said: "Do you stand or are you made to stand?" So the man stood up. It was said to him: "Do you say this to a jurist?" He said: "Iblis was more of a jurist than him. He said: 'My Lord, because You have led me astray,' while he (the Qadarite) says: 'I lead myself astray.'"

Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on surah 7, verse 17:

﴿Then I will surely come to them from before them﴾: I will cast doubt upon them regarding the Hereafter. ﴿And from behind them﴾: I will make them desire this world. ﴿And from their right﴾: from the direction of good deeds. ﴿And from their left﴾: from the direction of evil deeds. "Shama'il" (left sides, the plural of "shimal," meaning left) (p-559) means: ﴿Then I will surely come to them﴾ from the four directions from which the enemy usually attacks.

It is related from Shaqiq: "There is no morning but that Satan sits in wait for me at four ambush points. From before me, he says: 'Do not fear, for Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.' So I recite: ﴿And indeed I am the Forgiving of those who repent, believe, and do righteousness﴾ [Ta-Ha: 82]. From behind me, he frightens me with the loss of those I leave behind, so I recite: ﴿And there is no creature on the earth but that upon Allah is its provision﴾ [Hud: 6]. From my right, he comes to me from the direction of praise, so I recite: ﴿And the best outcome is for the righteous﴾ [al-A'raf: 128]. From my left, he comes to me from the direction of desires, so I recite: ﴿And a barrier will be placed between them and what they desire﴾ [Saba': 54]."

He did not say "from above them and from below them," because of the place of mercy and prostration. For the first two directions he used "min" (from), to indicate the starting point (ibtida' al-ghayah, the point from which an action begins), and for the last two he used "'an" (away from), because "'an" indicates deviation. ﴿And You will not find most of them grateful﴾: believing. He said this on the basis of conjecture and was correct, due to His words: ﴿And Iblis had already confirmed his assumption about them﴾ [Saba': 20]. Alternatively, he heard it from the angels through Allah's informing them.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 18:

﴿Said: Get out of it﴾ from the Garden, or from the heaven. "Madhu'um" (disgraced, censured), from dha'amahu, meaning he censured him; al-dha'm and al-dhamm both mean blame.

﴿Mad'hur﴾ (expelled, cast out), distanced from the mercy of Allah. The lam in ﴿whoever follows you among them﴾ is a preparatory lam (muwatti'ah) for the oath, and its answer is ﴿I will surely fill Hell﴾, which stands in place of the answer to the conditional clause. ﴿From you﴾ means from you (the addressee) and from them, so the pronoun of the addressee is given precedence (taghlib). ﴿All of you﴾.

﴿And O Adam﴾, and We said: "O Adam," after Iblis had been expelled from the Garden. ﴿Dwell, you and your wife, in the Garden﴾, take it as your dwelling place. ﴿And eat from wherever you wish, but do not approach this tree, or you will become﴾, that is, become, ﴿among the wrongdoers﴾.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 20:

﴿فَوَسْوَسَ لَهُما الشَيْطانُ﴾ "Waswasa" (to whisper, to murmur): when one speaks a hidden speech, repeating it while not being composed (in one's speech). A man is "muwaswis" with a kasra on the waw, and one does not say "muwaswas" with a fatha, but rather "muwaswas lahu" and "muwaswas ilayhi." The latter is the one into whom the whispering is cast. The meaning of "waswasa lahu" is: he performed the whispering for his sake, and "waswasa ilayhi" is: he cast it to him.

﴿لِيُبْدِيَ لَهُما ما وُورِيَ عَنْهُما مِن (p-٥٦٠)سَوْآتِهِما﴾ That He might expose to them what was concealed from them of their private parts. In it is evidence that uncovering the private parts is among the great matters, and that it has always been considered repugnant in natures and intellects. If you say: why was the damma-vowelled waw in "wūriya" not changed into a hamza, as in "uways," the diminutive of "wāṣil," whose original form is "wuwayṣil," so that the waw was changed into a hamza out of dislike of the coming together of two waws? I say: because the second is a madda (long vowel), like the alif of "wārā." Just as its hamza was not obligatory in "wāʿada," so it was not obligatory in "wūriya." This is because when two waws are both vowelled, there appears in them a heaviness that does not exist when the second is sukun. This is perceived necessarily, so they committed to changing it in the place of heaviness and not elsewhere. And ʿAbd Allah recited "ūriya" with the transposition (qalb). 

﴿وَقالَ ما نَهاكُما رَبُّكُما عَنْ هَذِهِ الشَجَرَةِ إلا أنْ تَكُونا مَلَكَيْنِ﴾ "And he said: Your Lord has forbidden you this tree only lest you become two angels," i.e., except out of dislike that you become two angels who know good and evil and are independent of food. It was recited "malikayn" (two kings), in accordance with His saying: ﴿وَمُلْكٍ لا يَبْلى﴾ [Ta-Ha: 120]. ﴿أوْ تَكُونا مِنَ الخالِدِينَ﴾ "or lest you become among the immortals," i.e., among those who do not die and remain dwelling in the Garden.

{Wa qasamahuma} means: and he swore to them. {Inni lakuma lamina al-nasihin} means: "Indeed I am to you both among the sincere advisors." The swearing of Iblis was expressed in the form of the verbal pattern (wazn) of mufa'ala (qasama), because the swearing came from him and the believing/acceptance came from them both, so it is as if it were from two parties.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 22:

﴿So he brought them down⟩ means He lowered them into eating from the tree. ﴿By deception⟩ means by what he deceived them with, namely the oath by Allah. Indeed, one deceives only a believer in Allah. And it is related from Ibn ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said: "Whoever deceives us by Allah, we are deceived by Him."

﴿When they tasted the tree⟩ means they found its taste, as they began eating from it. It was the ear of grain (sunbulah), or the grapevine (karm).

﴿Their private parts became apparent to them⟩ means their nakedness became visible to them, as the clothing fell away from them. They had not seen it from themselves, nor did either of them see it from the other. It was also said: their clothing was of the same kind as fingernails, meaning white like a fingernail, extremely fine and soft. So it remained on their fingernails as a reminder of the blessings and a renewal of regret. ﴿And they began﴾ means they set about it. It is said: "taffaqa yafʿalu kadha," meaning "he began to do such-and-such."

﴿Covering themselves with leaves from the Garden⟩ means they placed upon their nakedness leaves of the fig tree or the banana tree, one leaf upon another, so that they might conceal themselves with them, as one stitches a sandal (takhsifu al-naʿl). ﴿And their Lord called out to them: Did I not forbid you from that tree?⟩ This is a rebuke from Allah and a reminder of the error. It is related that He said to Adam, peace be upon him: "Did you not have, among the trees of the Garden which I bestowed upon you, a sufficient alternative to this tree?" He said: "Yes, but I did not think that anyone would swear falsely by You." He said: "By My might, I will surely bring you down to the earth. Then you will not attain livelihood except through toil of the hand and sweat of the brow." So he was brought down, and he was taught the craft of iron, and he was commanded to till the land, so he tilled, irrigated, harvested, threshed, winnowed, ground, kneaded, and baked.

﴿And I said to you both: Indeed Satan is a manifest enemy to you⟩

"They said: Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves, and if You do not forgive us and have mercy on us, we will surely be among the losers." In this there is evidence for us against the Mu'tazila, because minor sins (saghair) are, in their view, already forgiven.

"He said: Go down, [all of you]. The address is in the plural form to Adam and Eve, because Iblis had already descended before them. It is also possible that he (Iblis) descended to the heaven, and then they all descended to the earth. ﴿Some of you are enemies to others﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: hostile to one another; Iblis is hostile to both of them, and they are hostile to him.

﴿And for you on the earth is a dwelling place﴾: a settling (istiqrār), or a place of settling.

﴿And enjoyment﴾: benefit and enjoyment of livelihood ﴿for a time﴾: until the end of your appointed terms.

It is narrated from Thabit al-Bunani: When Adam, peace be upon him, was made to descend, and his death approached, the angels surrounded him, and Hawwa' began to circle around them. He said to her: "Leave my Lord's angels alone; what befell me, befell me because of you." When he died, the angels washed him with water and lote-tree leaves, an odd number of times, and embalmed him, and shrouded him in an odd number of garments. They dug a grave for him and made a lahd (niche) in it, and buried him in Sarandib, in the land of India. And they said to his children: "This is your sunnah (practice) after him."

﴿He said: "Therein you shall live﴾ on the earth, ﴿and therein you shall die, and from it you shall be brought forth﴾ for reward and punishment. (تَخْرُجُونَ, tukhrajūna, "you shall be brought forth") is read by Hamzah and ʿAlī.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 26:

﴿O children of Adam, We have sent down to you clothing﴾ He made what is on the earth a place of descent from the sky, because its origin is from water, and it is from it. ﴿to cover your private parts﴾ that conceals your nakedness.

﴿and as an adornment (rish)﴾ The clothing of adornment is borrowed from the rish (plumage) of birds, because it is their clothing and their adornment. That is: We sent down to you two kinds of clothing: clothing that covers your private parts, and clothing that adorns you.

﴿And the clothing of piety﴾ and the clothing of scrupulousness, which protects from punishment. It is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate (khabar) is the sentence: ﴿that is better﴾. It is as if it was said: "And the clothing of piety, it is better," because demonstratives (asma' al-isharah) draw close to pronouns in what refers back to a previously mentioned thing. Or "that" (dhalika) is an attribute (sifah) of the subject, and "better" (khayr) is the predicate of the subject, as if it was said: "And the clothing of piety, the one referred to, is better." Or "the clothing of piety" is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "It is the clothing of piety," that is, covering the nakedness is the clothing of the God-fearing. Then He said: "that is better." It has also been said: the clothing of the people of piety is of wool and coarse material. (And "wa-libasa al-taqwa", with the accusative, is read by Madani, Shami and 'Ali, as a conjunction over "libasan" and "rishan", meaning: and We sent down to you the clothing of piety.)

﴿That is among the signs of God﴾ which point to His grace and mercy towards His servants, meaning: the sending down of clothing. ﴿that perhaps they may take heed﴾ so that they may recognise the great blessing in it. This verse comes as a digression (istitrad) following the mention of the exposure of the private parts and the Adam and Eve's covering them with leaves, to show the favour in what has been created of clothing, and because of the disgrace in nakedness, and to indicate that concealment is part of piety.

[p. 563]

﴿O children of Adam, let not Satan tempt you as he removed your parents from the Garden, stripping them of their clothing﴾: he should not deceive you, nor lead you astray by keeping you from entering the Garden, just as he tempted your parents by causing them to be removed from it. ﴿Stripping them of their clothing﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl, a clause describing the state of the subject at the time of the action). That is, he removed them while stripping off their clothing, in that he was the cause of their clothing being taken from them. The prohibition is, on its surface, addressed to Satan, but in meaning it is addressed to the children of Adam, that is: do not follow Satan, lest he tempt you. ﴿To show them their private parts﴾, meaning their nakedness. ﴿Indeed, he﴾: the pronoun refers to the matter and the statement (the "shaʾn," a pronoun of the situation). ﴿Sees you, he﴾ is a justification (taʿlīl, giving the reason) for the prohibition and a warning against his temptation, since he is like an enemy who conceals his hostility, plotting against you from where you do not perceive. ﴿And his host﴾: his offspring or his armies among the devils. It is conjoined (ʿaṭf, grammatical coordination) to the pronoun in "yarākum" (sees you), which is emphasized by "huwa." It was not coordinated to that pronoun directly, because the object of the verb is the concealed (implicit) pronoun (mustakinn), not this overt one (bāriz). Coordination is only made to what is the object of the verb. ﴿From where you do not see them.﴾ Dhu'l-Nun said: If he sees you from where you do not see him, then seek help from the One who sees him from where he does not see him, and He is Allah, the Generous, the Concealer, the Merciful, the Forgiver.

﴿Indeed, We made the devils allies of those who do not believe﴾: in this there is an indication of the creation of acts (khalq al-afʿāl, the doctrine concerning whether God creates human actions).

﴿And when they commit an abomination﴾: that is, the sins whose ugliness is most emphasized. It is their circumambulating the House naked and their associating partners with God. ﴿They say, "We found our fathers doing it, and God has commanded us to do it."﴾ That is, when they committed these acts, they offered two excuses: that their forefathers used to do them, so they followed them, and that God had commanded them to do them, since He approved of them for them. For if He disliked them, He would have forbidden them from them. Both of these are false. The first is the blind imitation (taqlid) of the ignorant, and the second is a fabrication against the Majestic. ﴿Say, "Indeed, God does not command abomination."﴾ For what is commanded must necessarily be good, although goodness has degrees, as is known in usul al-fiqh (principles of jurisprudence). ﴿Do you say about God what you do not know?﴾ This is a rhetorical question of denunciation and reproach.

Say: "My Lord has commanded justice," meaning equity, and what is good in the eyes of every person of sound mind. So how could He command indecency?! "And set your faces (toward Him) at every place of prostration," "and" say: "set your faces" means: direct your worship to Him, upright toward it, not turning aside to anything else at every time of prostration, or at every place of prostration. "And call upon Him," that is, worship Him, "devoting religion to Him" (p-564), meaning: obedience, seeking thereby His sole Face. "As He originated you, so you will return." As He brought you into being at the beginning, so He will restore you. He argued against them in their denial of resurrection by the beginning of creation. The meaning is: He will restore you and recompense you for your deeds, so devote worship to Him sincerely.

"A party He guided," meaning the Muslims. "And a party—" that is, He let go astray a party, "upon whom error was justly decreed," meaning the disbelievers. "Indeed they," that is, indeed the party upon whom error was decreed, "took the devils as protectors apart from Allah," meaning helpers, "and they think that they are guided." And this verse is a proof for us against the Mu'tazila concerning guidance and misguidance.

O children of Adam, take your adornment at every place of prostration (masjid)—whenever you pray. And it has been said: the adornment (zina) is the comb and perfume. The sunnah is that a man take his best appearance for prayer, because prayer is intimate conversation with the Lord; so it is recommended to adorn oneself and to use perfume, just as covering the body and purifying oneself are obligatory.

﴿And eat﴾ of the meat and the fat.

﴿And drink and do not be excessive﴾ by engaging in what is forbidden, or by going beyond satiety. ﴿Indeed, He does not love those who are excessive.﴾ It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father: Eat whatever you wish, drink whatever you wish, and wear whatever you wish, so long as two things do not reach you: extravagance (israf) and arrogance (makhilah).

Al-Rashid had a skilled Christian physician, and he said to ʿAli ibn al-Husayn ibn Waqid: "There is nothing in your Book of the science of medicine; knowledge is of two kinds, the knowledge of bodies and the knowledge of religions." ʿAli said to him: "Allah has gathered all of medicine in half a verse of His Book, which is His saying: ﴿And eat and drink, but do not be excessive﴾." The Christian said: "Nothing has been transmitted from your Messenger about medicine." He said: "Our Messenger gathered medicine in brief words, which is his saying, peace and blessings be upon him: 'The stomach is the house of disease, restraint (al-himya) is the head of every remedy, and give every body what it has been accustomed to.'" The Christian said: "Your Book and your Prophet have left nothing of medicine for Galen."

Then he asked in denial of those who forbid what is lawful, saying: ﴿Say: Who has forbidden the adornment of Allah﴾ from clothing and everything else with which one beautifies oneself, ﴿which He has brought forth for His servants﴾, meaning its origin, namely cotton from the earth and silk from the silkworm, ﴿and the good things of provision﴾, the delicious foods and drinks. It was also said: when they entered the state of ihram, they forbade the sheep and what comes from its meat, its fat, and its milk.

﴿Say: They are for those who believe in the life of this world﴾, not exclusively for them, because the polytheists share them in it, ﴿exclusively on the Day of Resurrection﴾, with no one sharing them with the believers. He did not say "for those who believe and for others," in order to draw attention to the fact that these things were created for the believers in the primary sense, while the disbelievers are followers of them.

As for ﴿خالصة﴾ (khālişatan) with a nominative vowel, it is read by Nafi', so it is a mubtada' (subject), whose khabar (predicate) is ﴿لِلَّذِينَ آمَنُوا﴾ (for those who believe). ﴿فِي الْحَيَاةِ الدُّنْيَا﴾ (in the life of this world) is a zarf (adverbial complement) of the predicate. Alternatively, ﴿خالصة﴾ is a second predicate, or the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "it is exclusive." Others read it in the accusative as a hal (circumstantial accusative) referring back to the pronoun in the zarf, which is the predicate, meaning: "it is established for those who believe in the life of this world, in the state of its being exclusive on the Day of Resurrection."

﴿Thus do We detail the signs﴾, We distinguish the lawful from the unlawful, ﴿for a people who know﴾ that He has no partner.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 33:

﴿Say: Indeed, my Lord has forbidden the indecencies﴾ (rabbiya): Hamzah (read it). "Al-fawahish" (indecencies): that whose ugliness has become excessive (tafahasha), i.e., has increased. ﴿Those of them that are apparent and those that are concealed﴾ — their secret and their public forms. ﴿And sin﴾ — i.e., drinking wine, or every sin.

﴿And transgression﴾ — oppression and arrogance.

﴿Without right﴾ is connected to "transgression" (al-baghy). The place (i'rab) of ﴿and that you associate with Allah that for which He has sent down no authority﴾ (sultanan), i.e., no proof, is in the accusative (naṣb), as if he said: He forbade the indecencies, and He forbade association (shirk). (Yunazzil) with the light (tashdid removed, i.e., yunzilu) is read by Makki and Basri. In it there is mockery, since it is not permissible that He would send down proof for associating with Him something else. ﴿And that you say about Allah what you do not know﴾ — and that you fabricate about Him and invent lies, such as regarding prohibition and other matters.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 34:

﴿And for every nation there is a term﴾: a specified time at which the punishment of annihilation (ʿadhab al-istiʾsal) will come upon them if they do not believe. This is a warning to the people of Makkah of the punishment that descends at a known term with God, just as it descended upon the (earlier) nations. ﴿So when their term comes, they cannot delay it by an hour, nor can they hasten it.﴾ It is restricted to "an hour" because it is the smallest unit used in expressing a respite (al-imhal).

O children of Adam, if there come to you messengers from among you, reciting to you My verses (﴿يا بَنِي آدَمَ إمّا يَأْتِيَنَّكُمْ﴾): "in" (in) is the conditional particle (إنِ الشَرْطِيَّةُ, in al-shartiyya, the conditional "in"), to which "ma" has been joined to emphasize the sense of the condition, because "ma" itself is used for conditioning; for this reason its verb is followed by the heavy nun or the light nun. ﴿رُسُلٌ مِنكم يَقُصُّونَ عَلَيْكم آياتِي﴾ means: they recite My books to you. The clause "yaqussuna 'alaykum" is in the position of a raised (marfu') qualifier (sifa) of "rusul." The response of the condition is: ﴿فَمَنِ اتَّقى﴾ whoever guards against shirk (associating partners with God) ﴿وَأصْلَحَ﴾ and sets right his deeds, from among you, ﴿فَلا خَوْفٌ عَلَيْهِمْ ولا هم يَحْزَنُونَ﴾ there is no fear for them, nor will they grieve. Originally, (فَلا خَوْفَ) is the reading of Ya'qub (Ya'qub, i.e., Ya'qub al-Hadrami, one of the ten canonical readers).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 36:

﴿And those who denied﴾ from among you ﴿Our signs and were arrogant toward them﴾ exalted themselves against faith in them ﴿those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever﴾

﴿Who, then, is more unjust﴾: who is more heinous in wrongdoing ﴿than one who fabricates a lie against Allah or denies His signs﴾: than one who invents speech attributed to Allah that He did not say, or denies what He said. ﴿Those will receive their portion from the Book﴾: what was decreed for them of provisions and lifespans.

﴿Until when Our messengers come to them﴾: the Angel of Death and his assistants. "Until" (ḥattā, a particle marking an endpoint) indicates the limit of their receiving their portion and fulfilling it. It is the ḥattā after which a new sentence begins, and the sentence here is the conditional clause (al-jumlah al-shartiyyah), namely ﴿when Our messengers come to them﴾ (p-٥٦٧) ﴿seizing them﴾: taking their souls. This is a ḥāl (circumstantial clause, describing the state of the subject) from the messengers, meaning: those who are causing them to die. The word "mā" in ﴿They will say, "Where is what you used to call upon"﴾ is written in the mushaf (the codex of the Qur'an) joined to "ayna" (where), although it should properly be written separately, because it is a mawṣūlah (a relative or conjunctive particle). The meaning is: "Where are the gods you used to worship?" ﴿besides Allah﴾ to defend you. ﴿They will say, "They have strayed from us"﴾: they have disappeared from us, so we do not see them. ﴿And they will bear witness against themselves that they were disbelievers﴾: they will acknowledge their disbelief using the language of testimony (shahādah), which serves to confirm the report.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 38:

﴿Qāla udkhulū﴾ (He will say, "Enter"). That is: God Most High will say on the Day of Resurrection to these disbelievers: ﴿Enter﴾ ﴿in the company of nations﴾. The phrase ﴿fī umam﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: being among a multitude of nations, accompanying them, ﴿who have passed away﴾, i.e., gone by, ﴿before you, of jinn and humankind﴾, of the disbelievers among the jinn and humankind, ﴿into the Fire﴾. The phrase ﴿fī al-nār﴾ is connected to ﴿udkhulū﴾ (enter). ﴿Every time a nation entered﴾ the Fire, ﴿it cursed its sister﴾, i.e., its counterpart in religion, meaning the one that went astray by following its example. ﴿Until, when they have all overtaken one another therein﴾ — its original form is tadārakū, meaning they followed one another closely and gathered together in the Fire; the tā' was changed to dāl and made quiescent for assimilation (idghām), then a hamzat al-waṣl was prefixed. ﴿All together﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). ﴿Their latter﴾ in rank, who are the followers and the lowly ones, ﴿will say of their former﴾ in rank, who are the leaders and the chiefs. The meaning of ﴿li-ūlāhum﴾ (of their former) is "on account of their former," because their address is to God, not to them. ﴿Our Lord, these have led us astray, so give them a double punishment of the Fire.﴾ (ḍi‘fan: multiplied.) ﴿He will say, "For each there is double"﴾ — for the leaders because of misguidance and enticement, and for the followers because of disbelief and imitation.

﴿But you do not know﴾ what each group among you has of punishment. (Abū Bakr reads ﴿lā yaʿlamūna﴾ with the yāʾ, meaning: each group does not know the measure of the punishment of the other group.)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 39:

﴿And the first of them will say to the last of them: "You had no superiority over us, so taste the punishment for what you used to earn."﴾ They connected this statement to God's words addressed to the lowly followers: ﴿For each there is double﴾ [al-A'raf: 38], meaning: it has thus been established that you have no superiority over us, and that we are equal in deserving the double punishment. ﴿So taste the punishment for what you used to earn﴾ by your earning and your disbelief (p-568). This is part of the speech of the leaders to the lowly followers, and there is no pause at "superiority" (fadl). Alternatively, it is part of God's speech to all of them, and the pause is at "superiority" (fadl).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 40:

﴿Indeed, those who denied Our signs and were arrogant toward them — the gates of heaven will not be opened for them﴾. That is: they will not be permitted to ascend to heaven so as to enter Paradise, since it is in heaven. Or: no righteous deed of theirs will ascend for them, and blessing will not descend upon them. Or: their souls will not ascend when they die, as the souls of the believers ascend to heaven. It is read with the ta' and with lightening (takhfif) by Abu 'Amr, and with the ya' along with it by Hamzah and 'Ali.

﴿And they will not enter Paradise until the camel passes through the eye of the needle﴾. Until the camel (al-ba'ir) enters the hole of the needle. That is: they will never enter Paradise, because He has attached it to something that will never happen. Al-khiyat and al-makhit: that with which one sews, namely the needle.

﴿And thus﴾, that is, in the same manner as the dreadful recompense that We have described, ﴿We recompense the criminals﴾, that is, the disbelievers, as indicated by their denial of the signs of God and their arrogance toward them.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 41:

﴿For them there will be a bed (mihad) of Hell, and above them coverings (ghawashin).﴾ Mihad: a bed/couch. Ghawashin: coverings, the plural of ghashiyah.

﴿Thus do We recompense the wrongdoers﴾ — those who wronged themselves through disbelief.

﴿And those who believe and do righteous deeds - We do not burden any soul except according to its capacity﴾, i.e., its ability. Al-taklif (imposing an obligation, meaning the requirement of something that involves hardship), i.e., difficulty.

﴿Those﴾, أُولَئِكَ, is the mubtada' (grammatical subject of a nominal sentence), and the khabar (predicate) is ﴿the companions of the Garden﴾. The whole sentence is the khabar of الَّذِينَ (alladhina, "those who"). The clause ﴿We do not burden any soul except according to its capacity﴾ is an i'tiraḍ (parenthetical insertion) between the mubtada' and the khabar. ﴿They therein will abide forever﴾.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on surah 7, verse 43:

﴿And We will remove whatever resentment (*ghill*) is in their breasts﴾, meaning rancour (*hiqd*) that existed between them in the world. So there remains among them only mutual affection and compassion. It is related from ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him: "Indeed, I hope that I, and ʿUthman, and Talha, and al-Zubayr, are among them."

﴿Rivers flow beneath them﴾: this is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from "*hum*" in "*suduriHim*" (p-569), and the element governing it is the meaning of the annexation (*idafa*). ﴿They will say: "Praise be to Allah, who guided us to this,"﴾ that is, to what is a means to this great triumph, which is faith. ﴿And we would not have been [guided]﴾: "*ma kunna*" without a *waw*, according to the Syrian reading, so that it is a clause explaining the first one. ﴿Had Allah not guided us, we would never have been guided.﴾ The *lam* here is for emphasising the negation, meaning: it would not have been right for us to be guided, had it not been for Allah's guidance. The answer to "*lawla*" is omitted, and what precedes it indicates it. ﴿Indeed, the messengers of our Lord came with the truth﴾: so this was a kindness to us and an admonition toward guidance, and we were guided. They say this out of joy at what they have attained and to manifest what they believed.

﴿And they will be called: "This is the Garden"﴾: "*an*" is the light form of the heavy one, its noun is omitted, and the clause after it is its predicate. Its estimated form is: "They were called, [saying] that it is, this is the Garden," and the *ha'* is the pronoun of the matter (*damir al-shan*); or it carries the meaning of *ay* ("that is"), as if it were said to them: ﴿This is the Garden﴾ ﴿which you have been made to inherit﴾, that is, which you have been given. It is a circumstantial clause from "*al-jannah*," and the element governing it is what is in "*tilka*" of the meaning of pointing (*ishara*). ﴿For what you used to do.﴾ He called it an inheritance because it is not earned by deeds; rather, it is pure bounty from Allah and His promise for acts of obedience, like inheritance from the deceased, which is not a recompense for anything but is a pure gift.

Shaykh Abu Mansur, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The Mu'tazila (a theological school that held that human beings create their own acts and that certain matters are binding on Allah) opposed Allah regarding what He informed of concerning Nuh, peace be upon him, the people of Paradise and Hell, and Iblis. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿He leads astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 31]. Nuh, peace be upon him, said: ﴿My counsel will not benefit you, even if I wish to advise you, if Allah wills to lead you astray﴾ [Hud: 34]. The people of Paradise said: ﴿And we would not have been guided had Allah not guided us﴾. The people of Hell said: ﴿Had Allah guided us, we would have guided you﴾ [Ibrahim: 21]. And Iblis said: ﴿Because You have led me astray﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 16].

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 44:

﴿And the companions of the Garden will call out to the companions of the Fire: "Indeed, we have found [to be true]"⌉ "Anna" is a lightened form of the heavy (thaqīla) "anna," or it is explanatory (mufassira). Likewise: ﴿that the curse of God is upon the wrongdoers﴾. ﴿What our Lord promised us﴾ of reward ﴿is true﴾ — "ḥaqqan" is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl). ﴿So have you found what your Lord promised﴾ of punishment ﴿to be true?﴾ Its implied construction is: "What your Lord promised you," so "kum" (you) is omitted, the indication being ﴿what our Lord promised us﴾ in it. They only said this to them out of gloating over the companions of the Fire and acknowledging the blessings of God Most High. ﴿They will say: "Yes."﴾ And [it is read] with a kasra on the ʿayn wherever it occurs: ʿAlī. (p-570)

﴿Then a caller will call out among them﴾ — a herald called out, and he is an angel who makes the people of the Garden and the Fire hear him — ﴿that the curse of God is upon the wrongdoers﴾. ("Anna la'nata") is read by Makkī, Shāmī, Ḥamzah, and ʿAlī.

﴿Those who turn away﴾ means they prevent, ﴿from the way of Allah﴾, meaning His religion, ﴿and seek to make it crooked﴾. The phrase ﴿وَيَبْغُونَها عِوَجًا﴾ has عِوَجًا as a second object (مَفْعُولٌ ثانٍ, maf'ūl thānī) of ﴿لَيَبْغُونَ﴾. That is, they seek for it crookedness and contradiction. ﴿And they, in the Hereafter﴾, meaning the Last Abode, ﴿are disbelievers﴾.

﴿And between them﴾: between Paradise and Hell, or between the two groups.

﴿a barrier﴾: this is the wall mentioned in His words: ﴿So a wall was set up between them﴾ [al-Hadid: 13]. ﴿And on the heights﴾ (al-A'raf): on the heights of the barrier. These heights belong to the wall that was set up between Paradise and Hell, and they are its upper parts. The word is the plural of ʿarf, which is borrowed from ʿarf al-faras (the mane of a horse) and ʿarf al-dik (the comb of a rooster).

﴿men﴾: from among the most excellent of the Muslims, or from among those who will be the last to enter Paradise, because their good deeds and bad deeds are equal. Or they are those whom one of their parents did not approve of, or the children of polytheists.

﴿They will recognise each﴾: from among the groups of the blessed and the wretched, ﴿by their marks﴾, that is, by their sign. It is said that the mark of the believers is the whiteness and radiance of their faces, and the mark of the disbelievers is the blackness of their faces and the blueness of their eyes.

﴿And they will call out﴾: that is, the people of the heights,

﴿to the companions of the Garden: "Peace be upon you"﴾: that is, that it is peace, or it means "Peace!" This is a greeting of congratulation from them to the people of Paradise. ﴿They have not entered it﴾: that is, the people of the heights. The clause has no place in the i'rab (grammatical analysis), because it is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf), as if a questioner asked about the people of the heights, and it was said: ﴿They have not entered it﴾. ﴿Yet they hope﴾ to enter it. Or the clause has a place in i'rab, being an attributive description (sifah) of ﴿men﴾.

When their eyes are turned toward the companions of the Fire, they say: "Our Lord, do not place us with the wrongdoing people."

And when their eyes are turned (﴿وَإذا صُرِفَتْ أبْصارُهُمْ﴾): the eyes of the companions of the Heights (al-A'raf). In it is an indication that a turner (ṣārif) turns their eyes so that they look and seek refuge (fa-yastaʿīdhū).

Toward (﴿تِلْقاءَ﴾) is an adverb of place (ẓarf), meaning in the direction of (nāḥiyata) the companions of the Fire (﴿أصْحابِ النارِ﴾), and they see what is in it of punishment. They say (﴿قالُوا﴾): "Our Lord, do not place us with the wrongdoing people (﴿رَبَّنا لا تَجْعَلْنا مَعَ القَوْمِ الظالِمِينَ﴾)." So they seek refuge in God and flee to His mercy that He not place them with them.

And the companions of the Heights (al-A'raf, the elevated place between Paradise and Hell) call out to men ﴿from the heads of the disbelievers, recognizing them by their marks﴾, saying: ﴿"Your gathering (of wealth) did not avail you"﴾, meaning the wealth, or your multitude and your assembling. The "ma" is negating. ﴿"And what you used to be arrogant about"﴾, meaning your arrogance against the truth and against people. Then they say to them:

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 49:

﴿Are these﴾ is a mubtada' (subject of a nominal sentence). ﴿Those whom﴾ is the khabar (predicate) of a hidden mubtada', its estimated form being: "Are these" are they ﴿those whom you swore﴾ (aqsamtum), i.e. you swore in the world, and those referred to are the poor among the believers, like Suhayb, Salman, and others of their kind.

﴿Allah will not let them attain His mercy﴾ is the answer (jawab) to "you swore," and it falls within the relative clause of "those whom." Its estimated form is: you swore concerning them that Allah would not let them attain His mercy, i.e. He would not admit them to Paradise, because you despised them for their poverty. Then it will be said to the people of the A'raf (the heights): ﴿Enter Paradise; no fear shall be upon you, nor shall you grieve﴾, and that is after they have looked at the two groups and recognized them by their marks (sima), and have said what they said.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on Surah 7, verse 50:

﴿And the companions of the Fire will call out to the companions of the Garden: "Pour out upon us some water"﴾. "An" is *mufassira* (explanatory, glossing a preceding phrase of speech), and in it is evidence that the Garden is above the Fire. ﴿Or from what Allah has provided you﴾ refers to other drinks besides water, since they are included in the scope of "pouring out". Alternatively, "or" is taken to mean the sense of "throw down upon us" ﴿from what Allah has provided you﴾, that is, from the food and fruits. This is like the statement of the poet:

*"I fed her straw and cold water."*

That is, "and I gave her drink." They asked for this even though they had despaired of being answered, because the bewildered person speaks with what is useful and with what is not useful.

﴿They will say: "Indeed, Allah has forbidden them to the disbelievers"﴾. This is the prohibition of withholding, as in ﴿And We had forbidden him the wet-nurses﴾ [al-Qasas: 12]. Here you pause (*taqif*) if you put in the nominative or accusative what follows it as a condemnation (*dhamm*), but if you put it in the genitive as a qualifier of "the disbelievers", then you do not pause.

(p-572)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 51:

﴿Those who took their religion as amusement and play﴾ — they declared lawful and unlawful whatever they wished. Or, "their religion" means their festival (ʿīd).

﴿And the life of this world deceived them﴾ — they were deluded by the length of their lifespan. ﴿So today We will forget them﴾ — We will leave them in the punishment. ﴿As they forgot the meeting of this their day, and as they used to deny Our signs﴾ — that is, like their forgetting and their denial.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 52:

﴿And indeed We brought them a Book which We have detailed⦆ — We distinguished its lawful and its unlawful, its admonitions, and its narratives.

﴿with knowledge﴾ — knowing the manner of detailing its rulings,

﴿as guidance and mercy﴾ — a accusative circumstantial phrase (ḥāl manṣūb) relating to ﴿We have detailed it﴾, just as ﴿with knowledge﴾ is a circumstantial phrase (ḥāl) relating to its nominative (marfūʿ) element, ﴿for a people who believe﴾.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 53:

﴿Do they await anything but its final outcome?﴾ (yantazirun, "they wait for")  ﴿Anything but its ta'wil﴾ (illa 'aqibata amrihi, "except the ultimate consequence of its matter"), and what it returns to (ya'ulu ilayhi) of making manifest its truthfulness, and the clear appearance of the soundness of what it declared of promise and threat.

﴿On the day its ta'wil comes, those who had forgotten it before will say﴾ (tarakuhu, "they abandoned it", wa-a'radu 'anhu, "and turned away from it") ﴿Indeed the messengers of our Lord came with the truth﴾ (ay: tabayyana, "it became clear", wa-sahha, "and it was established", annahum ja'u bil-haqq, "that they had come with the truth"), so they acknowledged it at a time when it would not benefit them.

﴿So do we have any intercessors who will intercede for us?﴾ (jawab al-istifham, "the answer to the interrogative"). ﴿Or can we be returned?﴾ (jumlah ma'tufah 'ala jumlah qablaha dakhilah ma'aha fi hukm al-istifham, "a clause conjoined to a preceding clause that is included with it under the rule of the interrogative"), as if it were said: "Do we have any intercessors, or can we be returned?" Its raf' (nominative case) is due to its occurring in a position suitable for a noun, as when you say at the outset: "Does Zayd strike?" Or it is conjoined on an implied reading: "Does any intercessor intercede for us, or can we be returned?"

﴿That we may do other than what we used to do﴾ (fa-na'mala, "so that we may act"; jawab al-istifham as well) ﴿They have lost their souls, and what they used to fabricate has strayed far from them﴾ (ma kanu ya'buduna min al-asnam, "the idols that they used to worship").

(p. 573) ﴿Indeed your Lord is God, who created the heavens and the earth in six days﴾. He meant the heavens and the earth and what is between them. He detailed this in Surat Fussilat (Ha Mim al-Sajda), namely from Sunday to Friday, so that the angels might be considered step by step, to inform that matters should be approached deliberately, because every act has its day, and because the creation of one thing after another is a stronger indication of a knowing, managing, willing Creator who directs it according to His choice and causes it to run according to His will. ﴿Then He established Himself﴾, meaning He took possession (istawla). He ascribed the taking of possession to the Throne, although He, glory be to Him, has possession of all creatures, because the Throne is the greatest and highest of them. ﴿Over the Throne﴾. Explaining the Throne as a couch and the istiwa' as settling, as the anthropomorphists (al-Mushabbiha) say, is false, because He, exalted is He, existed before the Throne and without a place, and He is now as He was, since change is a attribute of created beings. What is transmitted from al-Sadiq, al-Hasan, Abu Hanifa and Malik, may God have mercy on them, is that the istiwa' is known, its modality (takyif) is unknown, belief in it is obligatory, denial of it is disbelief, and asking about it is an innovation (bid'ah). ﴿He covers the night with the day﴾. (Yughashshi) is read by Hamza, Ali and Abu Bakr. That is, He makes the night overtake the day and the day overtake the night. ﴿Seeking it rapidly﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to the night, meaning swiftly. The seeker is the night; as if, because of its swift passing, it seeks the day. ﴿And the sun and the moon and the stars﴾, that is, and He created the sun, the moon and the stars. ﴿Subjected﴾ is a circumstantial clause, meaning made subservient. (The sun and the moon and the stars are subjected) is the reading of al-Shami (Ibn Amir); here "the sun" is the subject (mubtada'), the rest are conjoined to it, and the predicate is ﴿subjected﴾. ﴿By His command﴾ is the command of bringing into being (amr takwin). When He mentioned that He created them subjected by His command, He said: ﴿Surely His is the creation and the command﴾, that is, He is the One who created things, and His is the command. ﴿Blessed be God﴾: His goodness has increased, or His beneficence endures. From barakah it means growth, or from buruk it means steadiness, and from it comes barakah,

﴿Lord of the worlds﴾.

﴿Call upon your Lord humbly and in secret﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: in a state of humility and secrecy. Taḍarruʿ is on the pattern tafaʿʿul (verb form V), from ḍarāʿah, which means abasement. It means with humbling and supplication.

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed you do not call upon one who is deaf or absent. You call upon One who is All-Hearing and near. He is with you wherever you are."

From al-Hasan: Between the supplication in secret and the supplication in public there is a seventy-fold difference.

﴿Indeed He does not love the transgressors﴾: those who exceed what they were commanded in every matter of supplication and other things.

From Ibn Jurayj: those who raise their voices in supplication. Also from him: shouting in supplication is disliked and an innovation (bidʿah, a newly introduced practice in religion). It was said: it is excessive verbosity in supplication.

From the Prophet (ﷺ): "There will be people who transgress in supplication. It is sufficient for a person to say: O Allah, I ask You for Paradise and whatever brings near to it of speech and action, and I seek refuge in You from the Fire and whatever brings near to it of speech and action." Then he recited: ﴿Indeed He does not love the transgressors﴾.

(p-574)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 56:

﴿And do not cause corruption on the earth after it has been set in order.﴾ That is: by disobedience after obedience, or by associating partners with God (shirk) after affirming His oneness (tawhid), or by wrongdoing (zulm) after justice (adl).

﴿And call upon Him in fear and in hope.﴾ These are two circumstantial qualifiers (hal), meaning: fearing rejection, hoping for response; or fearing the Fire and hoping for the Gardens; or fearing separation and hoping for reunion; or fearing the unseen outcome and hoping for the apparent guidance; or fearing justice and hoping for grace (fadl). ﴿Indeed, the mercy of God is near to the good-doers.﴾ The word "near" (qarib) is given in the masculine form on the interpretation that mercy (rahma) means the womb (rahim), or means compassion (tarahhum); or because it is an adjective of an omitted noun, that is, "a thing that is near"; or by analogy with the form fa'il, which has the meaning of maf'ul; or [because the feminine gender of "mercy" is not real (ghayr haqiqi)]; or because of its being attributed to a masculine noun (al-idafa ila al-mudhakkar).

﴿It is He who sends the winds﴾ (al-rīḥu, in the singular) is the reading of Makkī, Ḥamza and ʿAlī. (bushran, "as good news") (nashran) is the reading of Ḥamza and ʿAlī, a verbal noun (maṣdar, the infinitive form of the verb) from nashara. Its accusative case (inṣiʿāb) is either because "sent" and "raised" (nasha'a) are close in meaning, so it is as if it were said, "He spread them out in spreading," or because it is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl), meaning "spread out." (bushuran) is the reading of ʿĀṣim, a lightened form of bushran, the plural of bashīr, because the winds bring good news of rain. (nushuran) is the reading of al-Shāmī, a lightened form of nushr, like rusul and rusl. It is the reading of the rest of the readers, the plural of nushūr, meaning they spread out the rain.

﴿before His mercy﴾, before His blessing, which is rain, one of the greatest of blessings. ﴿Until, when they have borne﴾ means carried and lifted up. The derivation of iqlāl (bearing up) is from qilla (smallness), because one who is able to lift something sees what he lifts as small.

﴿heavy clouds﴾ heavy with water, the plural of saḥāba (cloud).

﴿We drive it﴾: the pronoun refers to the clouds according to the wording. Had it been taken according to the meaning, as with "heavy," it would have been feminine, just as if the adjective had been taken according to the wording it would have been said thaqīlan (masculine).

﴿to a dead land﴾ for the sake of a land in which there is no rain, and for watering it. (mayyit) is the reading of Madanī, Ḥamza, ʿAlī and Ḥafṣ.

﴿then We send down by it water﴾ by means of the clouds, or by means of the driving. Likewise, ﴿then We bring out by it every kind of fruit﴾, ﴿thus﴾ like that bringing out, which is the bringing out of fruits.

﴿Thus do We bring out the dead, so that you may remember﴾: then remembrance leads you to belief in resurrection, since there is no difference between the two bringings out, because each of them is the return of a thing after its production.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 58:

﴿And the good land – its vegetation comes forth by the permission of its Lord.﴾ That is, the land whose soil is good. ﴿By the permission of its Lord﴾ means by His facilitation. This phrase is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), as if it were said: its vegetation comes forth good and abundant, because it stands in contrast to "nakidan" (meagre). ﴿And as for that which is corrupt﴾ is a descriptive attribute of the land, meaning: and the corrupt land.

﴿It does not come forth﴾ that is, its vegetation, and it is omitted because of what is understood. ﴿Except meagrely﴾ – that which has no good in it. This is a parable for the one in whom admonition takes effect, who is the believer, and for the one upon whom nothing of that has any effect, who is the disbeliever. This illustration follows on from the parable of that rain, its descent upon the dead land, and the bringing forth of fruits by it, by way of digression (istiṭrād).

﴿Thus﴾ like that disposition ﴿We vary the signs﴾ – We repeat them and reiterate them.

﴿For a people who give thanks﴾ for the favour of Allah – and they are the believers – so that they may reflect upon them and take lessons from them.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 59:

﴿Indeed We sent﴾ is the answer to an omitted oath, meaning: by Allah, ﴿Indeed We sent Noah to his people﴾. He was sent when he was fifty years old, and he was a carpenter. He is Noah son of Lamak son of Mutawshalakh son of Akhnukh (Enoch), and Akhnukh is the name of Idris, peace be upon him. ﴿So he said: "O my people, worship Allah; you have no god other than Him."﴾ The reading of "ghayruhu" and "ghayrihi" (in the genitive) is from ʿAli. The nominative is on the basis of the position (al-mahall), as if it were said: "You have no god other than Him, so do not worship anything alongside Him." The genitive is on the basis of the wording (al-lafz).

﴿Indeed, I fear for you the punishment of a great day﴾, which is the Day of Resurrection, or the day the punishment descends upon them, and it is the Flood.

The chiefs (al-mala'), i.e., the nobles and leaders, from among his people said: ﴿Indeed, we see you in manifest error.﴾ That is, clearly astray, having gone away from the path of rectitude. And "seeing" (al-ru'yah) here is seeing of the heart (ru'yat al-qalb), i.e., judgment and conviction rather than sight of the eye.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 61:

﴿He said: "O my people, there is no misguidance in me"﴾. He did not say "ḍalāl" as they had said, because ḍalāla (misguidance) is more specific than ḍalāl (error/going astray), so it is more emphatic in negating misguidance from himself. It is as if he had said: "There is not in me any part of ḍalāl." Then he added a corrective clause to reinforce the negation of ḍalāla, saying: ﴿but I am a messenger from the Lord of the worlds﴾, because his being a messenger from God, conveying His message, amounts to his being upon the straight path, and so he was at the utmost degree of guidance.

"I convey to you the messages of my Lord," meaning what was revealed to me over extended periods, or in its various meanings: commands, prohibitions, admonitions, good tidings, and parallels.

(أُبْلِغُكُمْ) is the reading of Abu 'Amr. This is a resumptive statement explaining that he is a messenger of the Lord of the worlds.

﴿And I give you sincere counsel﴾: I intend your welfare with sincerity. It is said: نَصَحْتُهُ and نَصَحْتُ لَهُ. The addition of the lam indicates emphasis and denotes the purity of the counsel (إمْحاضِ النَصِيحَةِ). The essence of sincere counsel (نُصْح) is wishing for another the good that you wish for yourself, or the utmost in sincere concern.

﴿And I know from God what you do not know﴾: that is, His attributes, meaning His overwhelming power, the severity of His seizing of His enemies, and that His might is not averted from the criminal people.

(p-577)

﴿Or are you amazed?﴾ The hamza (ء, the interrogative particle) here expresses denial, and the waw (و, the conjunction) signifies coordination (ʿatf). The element coordinated with is omitted, as if it had been said: "Do you deny and are you amazed?!" ﴿that there came to you﴾ from ﴿that there came to you﴾ ﴿a reminder﴾, meaning an admonition ﴿from your Lord through a man from among you﴾, that is, through the tongue of a man from among you, i.e., of your own kind. This is because they used to marvel at the prophethood of Nuh (peace be upon him) and would say: ﴿We have not heard of this among our forefathers of old﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 24], meaning: the sending of a human being.

﴿Had God willed, He would have sent down angels﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 24] ﴿to warn you﴾, to caution you about the consequence of disbelief, ﴿and that you may be mindful of God﴾, that taqwa (God-consciousness, which is fear that arises from the warning) may come to be found among you.

﴿And perhaps you will be shown mercy﴾: that you may be shown mercy through taqwa, if it is found in you.

**﴿So they denied him﴾** — they attributed to him lying. **﴿So We saved him and those with him﴾** — and they were forty men and forty women; it is also said nine: his sons Sam, Ham, and Japheth, and six of those who believed in him. 

**﴿in the ship﴾** — this is connected to "with him," as if it were said: "and those who accompanied him in the ship."

**﴿And We drowned those who denied Our signs. Indeed they were a blind people﴾** — blind to the truth. It is said: *a'ma* (ﺃَعْمَى) is used of the sight, and *ama* (عَمٍ) of the insight (basirah).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 65:

﴿And to ʿĀd﴾: We sent to ʿĀd. It is coordinated (ʿaṭf) upon ﴿Nuh﴾. ﴿Their brother﴾: one of them, as in your saying, "O brother of the Arabs," addressed to one of them. He was made one of them because the message from a man of their own is more intelligible to them, so the proof against them is more binding.

﴿Hud﴾: an appositive (ʿaṭf bayān) to "their brother." He is Hud son of Shalikh son of Arfakhshadh son of Sam son of Nuh.

﴿He said: O my people, worship Allah; you have no god other than Him. Will you not then be wary?﴾ He did not say "fa-qala" (then he said), as in the story of Nuh (peace be upon him), because it is in the sense of answering a questioner who said: "What did Hud say to them?" So it was said: "He said, O my people, worship Allah." And likewise:

﴿The chiefs of those of his people who disbelieved said﴾. The commentator says that the chiefs are described as "those who disbelieved" rather than simply "the chiefs" as in the case of the people of Noah (peace be upon him), because among the nobles of the people of Hud (peace be upon him) there were those who believed in him, among them Marthad ibn Sa'd (p-٥٧٨). So the distinction was intended through the description, and there was no believer among the nobles of the people of Noah (peace be upon him).

﴿Indeed, we see you in folly﴾: in lightness of judgment and feebleness of intellect, in that you abandon the religion of your people for another religion. The word "folly" (safahah, سَفاهَةٍ) is used as a container in a figurative sense (majaz), meaning that he is firmly established in it and not separated from it. ﴿And indeed, we think you are among the liars﴾, in your claim to prophethood.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verses 67–68:

﴿He said, "O my people, there is no folly in me, but I am a Messenger from the Lord of the worlds.﴾ ﴿I convey to you the messages of my Lord, and I am a sincere adviser to you in what I call you to,﴾ ﴿trustworthy﴾ regarding what I tell you. As for his saying here, ﴿"and I am a sincere adviser to you, trustworthy,"﴾ it is because of their saying: ﴿"And indeed, we think you are among the liars,"﴾ that is, so that the noun (ism) may correspond to the noun (ism).

In the response of the Prophets, peace be upon them, to those who attribute to them misguidance and folly, with what they answered them, of speech that proceeds from forbearance, overlooking, and refraining from retaliating with what they said to them, despite their knowledge that their opponents are the most misguided and foolish of people, there is a good manner and a great character. God Most High's report of that is an instruction to His servants on how to address the foolish, how to overlook them, and how to let their skirts trail over what comes from them.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verses 67–68:

﴿He said, "O my people, there is no folly in me, but I am a Messenger from the Lord of the worlds.﴾ ﴿I convey to you the messages of my Lord, and I am a sincere adviser to you in what I call you to,﴾ ﴿trustworthy﴾ regarding what I tell you. As for his saying here, ﴿"and I am a sincere adviser to you, trustworthy,"﴾ it is because of their saying: ﴿"And indeed, we think you are among the liars,"﴾ that is, so that the noun (ism) may correspond to the noun (ism).

In the response of the Prophets, peace be upon them, to those who attribute to them misguidance and folly, with what they answered them, of speech that proceeds from forbearance, overlooking, and refraining from retaliating with what they said to them, despite their knowledge that their opponents are the most misguided and foolish of people, there is a good manner and a great character. God Most High's report of that is an instruction to His servants on how to address the foolish, how to overlook them, and how to let their skirts trail over what comes from them.

﴿Do you wonder that a reminder from your Lord has come to you through a man from among you, so that he may warn you? And remember when He made you successors (khulafa') after the people of Noah﴾. That is, you left them behind in the earth, or in their dwellings. "Idh" is a direct object (maf'ul bihi), not an adverb of time (zarf). The meaning is: remember the time of your succession.

﴿And He increased you in creation in stature (basta)﴾: in length and height. So the shortest of them was sixty cubits, and the tallest was a hundred cubits. The reading (بَصْطَةً) is that of al-Hijazi, 'Asim, and 'Ali.

﴿So remember the bounties (ala') of God﴾: in your succession, in the expansion of your bodies, and in whatever else of His gifts. The singular of ala' is ilan (إلى), like inan and ana'in (إنى وآناءٍ). ﴿That you may prosper﴾

(p-٥٧٩)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 70:

The meaning of "coming" in: ﴿They said: Have you come to us?﴾ is that Hud, peace be upon him, had a secluded place away from his people in which he would practise tahannuth (spiritual retreat and devotion, seeking purity away from idolatry), just as the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to do at Hira' before the prophethood. When revelation came to him, he came to his people calling them ﴿to worship Allah alone and to abandon what our fathers used to worship﴾. They denied this and considered it far-fetched that Allah alone should be singled out for worship, and that the religion of the fathers, which involved taking idols as partners alongside Him, should be abandoned, out of love for what they had been brought up upon. ﴿So bring us what you threaten us with﴾ of punishment ﴿if you are of the truthful﴾ in claiming that the punishment is about to descend upon us.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 71:

﴿He said: Indeed there has befallen﴾ i.e., it has already descended ﴿upon you﴾. He made the expected (what must inevitably descend) to be as the occurred, like your saying to one who has asked you for some requests: "It has already been done." ﴿from your Lord, an abomination﴾ a punishment, ﴿and wrath﴾ indignation, ﴿Do you dispute with me concerning names you have named﴾ concerning things which are nothing but names with no named realities beneath them, because you call the idols "gods" while they are empty of the meaning of divinity, ﴿you and your fathers, for which Allah has sent down no authority﴾ no proof. ﴿So wait﴾ for the descent of the punishment, ﴿indeed I am with you among those who wait﴾ for that.

﴿So We delivered him and those with him﴾, meaning those who believed in him, ﴿by a mercy from Us, and We cut off the last remnant of those who denied Our signs﴾. The *dabir* (remnant, last of the line) means the root, or that which is behind a thing. Cutting off their *dabir* means their annihilation and their destruction down to the last of them.

﴿And they were not believers﴾. The benefit of this is the negation of faith from them, together with affirming that they denied the signs of God. This indicates that destruction was specific to those who denied.

Their story: the 'Ad had spread throughout the lands between 'Oman and Hadramawt, and they had idols they worshipped: Sida', Sumud and al-Haba'. God sent Hud to them, and they denied him, so He withheld rain from them for three years. Whenever a calamity befell them, they would seek relief from God at His Sacred House, so they dispatched to it Qayl ibn 'Anz, Laqim ibn Huzal, and Martha ibn Sa'd, who concealed his faith in Hud (peace be upon him). The people of Mecca at that time were the 'Amaliq, the sons of 'Imliq ibn Lawadh ibn Sam ibn Nuh, and their chief was Mu'awiya ibn Bakr. They alighted with him on the outskirts of Mecca, and Martha said to them: "You will not be given water until you believe in Hud." So they left Martha behind and departed. Qayl said: "O God, give water to 'Ad as You used to give it to them." So God produced three clouds: white, red and black. Then a caller called out to him from the sky: "O Qayl, choose for yourself and your people." He chose the black, supposing it contained the most water. It went out over 'Ad from their valley, and they rejoiced and said: "This is a cloud bringing us rain." But a barren wind came from it and destroyed them, while Hud and the believers with him were saved. They came to Mecca, worshipped God there, until they died.

And We sent [to] ﴿Thamud﴾. It was also read as ﴿wa-ila Thamudin﴾ (with the kasra on the final letter), by interpreting it as the living group (ta'wil al-hayy, interpretation of the name as referring to a people), or by considering its origin (asl), since it is the name of their eldest forefather. The non-declension (man' al-sarf, the withholding of tanwin and the kasra in the diptote form) is by interpreting it as a tribe (qabila). It was said: they were named Thamud because of the scarcity of their water, from al-thamad, which is little water. Their dwellings were al-Hijr, between the Hijaz and al-Sham (Syria).

﴿Their brother Salih. He said: "O my people, worship Allah; you have no god other than Him. There has certainly come to you a clear proof from your Lord."﴾ A manifest sign, bearing witness to the truth of my prophethood. It is as if it was asked: "What is this proof?" So he said: ﴿"This is the she-camel of Allah"﴾. This is an idafa (genitive construction) of specification and honour, because she came into being by His creation, may He be exalted, without a father or a womb.

﴿"For you, a sign"﴾: a hal (circumstantial accusative) from the she-camel, and the governing element is the meaning of the demonstrative "this". It is as if it was said: "She was pointed out as a sign." "For you" is an explanation of those for whom she is a sign, namely Thamud, because they witnessed her directly.

﴿"So leave her to eat in the land of Allah"﴾, that is: the land is the land of Allah and the she-camel is the she-camel of Allah. So leave her to eat in the land of her Lord, from the plants of her Lord; there is no burden of her upkeep upon you. ﴿"And do not touch her with harm"﴾ (p-٥٨١): do not strike her, do not hamstring her, and do not drive her away, out of honour for the sign of Allah. ﴿"Lest a painful punishment seize you"﴾: ﴿فَيَأْخُذَكُمْ﴾ is the answer (jawab) to the prohibition.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on Surah 7, verse 74:**

﴿And remember when He made you successors after ʿĀd and settled you in the land﴾ and lodged you; al-mabāʾa means the dwelling place. ﴿in the land﴾, in the land of al-Ḥijr, between al-Ḥijāz and al-Shām.

﴿You take from its plains palaces﴾, upper chambers for the summer, ﴿and you hew the mountains into houses﴾ for the winter. "Houses" is a ḥāl muqaddara (an anticipated circumstantial qualifier, a state that is to come about), as in the phrase "Tailor this garment as a shirt" (khuṭṭa hādhā al-thawba qamīṣan), since the mountain is not a house while it is being hewn, nor is the garment a shirt while it is being sewn.

﴿So remember the bounties of God and do not run riot in the land, causing corruption﴾. It is related that when ʿĀd was destroyed, Thamūd inhabited its lands and succeeded them in the land, and they were given long lifespans. So they hewed houses out of the mountains, fearing their collapse before death. They lived in ease and comfort, so they transgressed against God, spread corruption in the land, and worshipped idols. God sent to them Ṣāliḥ, and they were an Arab people; Ṣāliḥ was among the best of them in lineage. He called them to God, but only a few of the weak among them followed him. He warned them, and they asked him to bring forth from a specific rock a pregnant she-camel (ʿushrāʾ). He prayed and called upon his Lord, and the rock writhed like a woman in labour with her child (al-natūj), and out of it came a she-camel just as they had asked. Jundaʿ and a group of his people then believed in him.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 75:**

﴿The eminent ones (al-mala') among his people who were arrogant said﴾ ("and he said," wa-qala) is the reading of al-Shami (Ibn ʿĀmir). ﴿to those who were oppressed﴾ means to those whom the leaders of the disbelievers had oppressed. ﴿to those of them who believed﴾ is a *badal* (substitute, or apposition, grammatically a restatement of the preceding noun) of "those who were oppressed," with the preposition repeated. This is evidence that a *badal* wherever it occurs is understood as having the governing word (*ʿamil*) repeated. The pronoun in "minhum" ("of them") refers to "qawmihi" ("his people").
