This indicates that their oppression was limited to the believers. Alternatively, it refers to "those who were oppressed," and this indicates that the oppressed were both believers and disbelievers.

﴿Do you know that Salih is one sent from his Lord?﴾ They said this mockingly. ﴿They said: Indeed we believe in that with which he was sent.﴾ This became their answer because they asked them about knowledge of his being sent, so they made his being sent a known and accepted matter, as if they had said: knowledge of his being sent, and of that with which he was sent, is beyond doubt. The discussion is only about the obligation to believe in him, so we inform you: we believe in him.

The arrogant among his people said: ﴿Indeed, we are disbelievers in that which you have believed.﴾ They placed ﴿you have believed in it﴾ in place of ﴿he has been sent with it﴾, as a rejection of what the believers had made known and accepted.

﴿So they hamstrung the she-camel﴾. He attributed the hamstringing to all of them, although the one who hamstrung her was Qudar ibn Salif, because it was done with their approval. Qudar was red-faced, blue-eyed and short, just as Pharaoh was. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "O Ali, the most wretched of the first (people) is the one who hamstrung the she-camel of Salih, and the most wretched of the last (people) is your killer."

﴿and they defied the command of their Lord﴾, meaning they turned away from it and were arrogant. "The command of their Lord" is what He commanded through the tongue of Salih, peace be upon him, namely His saying: ﴿So leave her to eat on Allah's earth﴾ [Al-A'raf: 73]. Or it means "the affair of their Lord," which is His religion.

﴿And they said, "O Salih, bring us what you threaten us with"﴾ of the punishment.

﴿"If you are among the messengers."﴾

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 78:

﴿So the convulsion seized them﴾: the *sayha* (the mighty cry) by which the earth was shaken, and they were convulsed by it. ﴿So they became in their home﴾: in their land, or their dwellings.

﴿Jathimin﴾: dead, sitting. It is said: "al-nas *juthumm*" (الناس جُثَّمٌ), meaning people sitting motionless (*la hirak bihim*, لا حِراكَ بِهِمْ), not speaking.

﴿So he turned away from them﴾ when they hamstrung the she-camel. ﴿And said, "O my people, I have certainly conveyed to you the message of my Lord and advised you, but you do not love those who advise"﴾ at the time of his parting from them. [The ones who] command guidance [are those who], for the sake of making desire sweet (li-istihla' al-hawa). Advice (al-nasihah) is a gift that wards off disgrace, but it is unpalatable and breeds resentment (al-sakhimah). It is related that their hamstringing of the she-camel took place on Wednesday. Salih said, "You will live three days after it: your faces will turn yellow on the first day, red on the second, black on the third, and the punishment will befall you on the fourth." And it was so. It is also related that he went out with one hundred and ten of the Muslims, weeping. When he learned that they had perished, he returned with those who were with him, and they settled in their dwellings.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 80:

﴿And Lut, when he said to his people﴾: meaning, remember Lut; and "idh" (when) is in apposition to it (badal) ﴿Do you commit the lewdness﴾: do you do the evil deed that is persisting in ugliness?! ﴿No one in the worlds has preceded you in it﴾: no one has done it before you. The "ba'" (bi) here is for transitivity (li'l-ta'diyah), and from this is the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "'Ukkashah has preceded you with it" ﴿of anyone﴾: "min" is extra (za'idah) for emphasizing the negation and conveying the meaning of comprehensiveness ﴿from among the worlds﴾: "min" is partitive (li'l-tab'id). This is a resumed sentence (jumlah mustanfa'ah), in which he first rebuked them with his saying ﴿Do you commit the lewdness﴾, and then reproached them for it, saying: you are the first to have done it.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 81:

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, you approach men﴾ ﴿Indeed, you approach men﴾ is an elucidation of His saying: ﴿Do you approach the abomination?﴾ The interrogative hamza (alif of interrogation) in "Atata'unna" [in the previous verse] serves the same function here, for denunciation. The reading ﴿innakum﴾ (with the hamza of inna pronounced as a statement, not a question) is that of Madani and Hafs. It is said: "Ataa al-mar'ah" (he approached the woman) means: he had intercourse with her (ghashiyahā).

﴿Lust﴾ (shahwatan) is an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), meaning: for the sake of desire, with no motive compelling you to it except mere lust. And there is no blame greater than this, because it describes them as having the nature of beasts (bahimiyyah).

﴿Instead of women﴾ (min dun al-nisa') means: not from women. ﴿Rather, you are a people who exceed the limits﴾ (bal antum qawmun musrifun). He turned away from denunciation to a statement about them, describing the condition that necessitates committing abominations, namely that they are a people whose habit is excess and transgressing limits in everything. Therefore they went to excess in the matter of satisfying desire, until they transgressed what is customary to what is not customary.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 82:

﴿And the answer of his people was only that they said, "Expel them from your town."﴾ That is: (p-584) Lut and those who believed with him. Meaning: they did not answer him with anything that would constitute a reply to what Lut had addressed to them, namely his denunciation of the abomination and his description of them with the attribute of excess (al-israf), which is the root of evil. Rather, they brought forward something unrelated to his speech and his admonition, namely the command to expel him and those believers with him from their town. ﴿Indeed, they are people who keep themselves pure﴾: they claim purity, they claim (to be free of) our wicked deed. From Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father: they reproached them with what is praised.

"So We saved him and his family, except for his wife; she was among those who remained behind." Here "his family" (أهله) refers to those specially connected to him among his kin, or among the believers. ﴿إلا امْرَأتَهُ كانَتْ مِنَ الغابِرِينَ﴾ — "except his wife; she was among those who remained behind," meaning among those who stayed behind in the punishment. The masculine form (الغابرين, "those who remained") is used to give precedence to the males over the females. She was a disbeliever, allied with the people of Sodom (Sadum). It is narrated that she looked back, and a stone struck her, and she died.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 84:

﴿And We rained upon them a rain﴾ — that is, We sent down upon them a rain of a strange kind. They said: Allah rained upon them brimstone (kibrit) and fire. It has also been said: He caused the earth to swallow up those of them who remained in their dwellings, and stones were rained upon those of them who were travelling. Abu 'Ubayda said: "amtara" (to rain) is used for punishment, and "matara" is used for mercy. ﴿So look how was the end of the criminals﴾ — the disbelievers.

and to Madyan [We sent] their brother Shu'ayb. "And" [We sent] "to Madyan," which is the name of a tribe. [Shu'ayb] "their brother." He is called "the orator of the prophets" (khatib al-anbiya') for the excellence of his argumentation with his people. They were people who cheated in measures and weights. He said, "O my people, worship Allah; you have no god other than Him. There has certainly come to you a clear proof from your Lord"; that is, a miracle, even if it is not mentioned in the Qur'an.

"So give full measure and weight": complete them. The intended meaning is: give full the measure and the weighing of the scale. Or "al-mizan" may be like "al-mi'ad" (appointment), in the sense of a verbal noun.

"And do not deprive people of their things": do not diminish their rights by cheating in measure and shortchanging in weight. They used to deprive people of everything in their dealings. "Bakhasa" (to deprive) transitively takes two objects: "al-nas" (the people) and "ashya'ahum" (their things). You say: "bakhastu Zaydan haqqahu," meaning, I diminished for Zayd his right, i.e., I reduced it for him.

"And do not cause corruption on the earth after its reformation": after its reform, that is, do not cause corruption in it after the righteous among the prophets and the friends of Allah have set it right. Its idafa (construction) is like the idafa in: "Rather, the plotting of the night and the day" [Saba' 33], meaning: rather, your plotting by night and day. "That" refers to what has been mentioned of fulfilling measure and weight, abstaining from depriving, and not causing corruption on the earth.

"is better for you" in humanity and in good repute,

"if you are believers," affirming what I say.

﴿Do not sit on every path﴾ (*bi-kulli ṭarīq*): on every road, ﴿threatening﴾ those who believe in Shu'ayb with punishment, ﴿and barring﴾ from ﴿the way of Allah﴾ (*ʿan al-ʿibāda*): from worship, ﴿those who believe in Him﴾ (*bi-Allāh*): in Allah. It is also said that they used to rob travellers, and it is said that they were tax collectors.

﴿and seeking to make it crooked﴾: and you seek for the way of Allah ﴿crookedness﴾ (*ʿiwajan*), that is, you describe it to the people as a crooked, non-straight way, so that you may prevent them from following it. The grammatical position (*maḥall*, i'rab) of ﴿threatening﴾ and what is conjoined to it is the accusative of circumstance (*al-ḥāl*), meaning: do not sit threatening, barring from the way of Allah, and seeking crookedness.

﴿And remember when you were few﴾: ﴿when﴾ (*idh*) is a direct object and not an adverb of time; that is, remember, by way of gratitude, the time when you were few in number. ﴿Then He multiplied you﴾: Allah multiplied and increased your number. It is also said that Madyan ibn Ibrahim married a daughter of Lut, and she bore children, and Allah cast blessing and growth into her offspring, so they became numerous.

﴿And see how was the end of the corrupters﴾: the final outcome of those who corrupted before you among the nations, such as the people of Nuh, Hud, Salih, and Lut, peace be upon them.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 87:

﴿And if there is a group among you who believe in that with which I have been sent, and a group who do not believe, then be patient﴾ until ﴿Allah judges between us﴾, i.e., between the two groups, by granting victory to the righteous (al-muhiqqin) over the falsifiers (al-mubtilin) and making them prevail over them. This is a threat to the disbelievers of retribution from Allah, the Exalted, against them. Or it is an exhortation to the believers to be patient and to endure what the polytheists would inflict upon them, until Allah judges between them and avenges them upon them. Or it is an address to both groups, meaning: let the believers be patient over the harm of the disbelievers, and the disbelievers be patient over what grieves them of the faith of those among them who believed, until Allah judges, distinguishing the wicked from the good. ﴿And He is the best of judges﴾, because His judgment is true and just, and injustice is not feared in it.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 88:

﴿The chiefs of those of his people who were arrogant said: "We will surely expel you, O Shu'ayb, and those who believed with you from our town, or you will return to our creed."﴾ That is: one of the two matters will certainly occur, either your expulsion or your returning to disbelief. "He said" Shu'ayb, ﴿"Even though we are averse?"﴾ The hamza is for interrogation (istifham), and the waw is for the circumstantial (hal), its estimated meaning being: "Will you return us to your creed while we are in a state of aversion, and while we are averse?" They said: "Yes."

Then Shu'ayb said: ﴿We would be fabricating a lie against God if we returned to your religion﴾. This is an oath, with the implied lam removed; that is, "By God, we would indeed be fabricating a lie against God if we returned to your religion ﴿after God has rescued us from it﴾," that is, God has delivered us from it. If you ask: how could Shu'ayb say ﴿if we returned to your religion﴾ when disbelief is impossible for the prophets, peace be upon them? I answer: he meant the return of his people, but he included himself among them, although he was innocent of that, in keeping his speech with the rule of taghlib (the grammatical principle of giving precedence to the majority or the dominant group).

﴿And it is not for us﴾, that is, it is not fitting for us, it is not valid for us,

﴿to return to it unless God, our Lord, wills﴾, that is, unless it has already been decreed in His will that we return to it, since all existing things, good and evil, are by the will of God, the Exalted. ﴿Our Lord encompasses all things in knowledge﴾: this is a tamyiz (specification of comparison), that is, He is knowing of everything; He knows the states of His servants, how they change, and how their hearts turn about.

﴿In God we have put our trust﴾, that He keep us firm in faith and grant us success in increasing certainty.

﴿Our Lord, decide between us and our people in truth﴾, that is, judge. The fataha (the act of opening, i.e., judging) is judgment and adjudication, and judging in truth opens what is closed, which is why it is called (p-587) fath (opening), and the people of Oman call the judge "fattah" (opener).

﴿And You are the best of those who decide﴾, like His saying: ﴿and He is the best of judges﴾.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 90:

﴿And the chiefs of those among his people who disbelieved said: "If you follow Shu'ayb, then indeed you will be losers."﴾ They will be defrauded (maghbunun) because of the loss of the benefits of cheating (bakhs) and short-measuring (tatfif) by following him, since he forbids you from both of them and makes you (adopt) full measure and fairness (al-iifa' wa-l-taswiya). The answer to the oath (jawab al-qasam), which the lam introduced in ﴿لَئِنِ اتَّبَعْتُمْ﴾ (la-in ittaba'tum, "If you follow"), and the answer to the condition (jawab al-shart) are both: 

﴿إنَّكم إذًا لَخاسِرُونَ﴾ (innakum idhan la-khasirun, "indeed you will be losers"). It therefore serves as the answer to both of them (sadd masadd al-jawabayn).

ﵠ"Then the earthquake seized them" — ar-rajfa: the quake, the violent shaking. "So they were in their abode in the morning, prostrate" — dead, lifeless.

Translation of the passage:

﴿فَأخَذَتْهُمُ الرَجْفَةُ﴾ — "So the earthquake (al-ratafa? no)..." 

Let me restate accurately:

﴿So the earthquake seized them﴾ — al-zalzala (the violent quake). ﴿So they were in their abode, lying prostrate﴾ — dead (mayyitin).

The Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 92:

﴿Those who denied Shu'ayb﴾ is a subject (mubtada'), whose predicate (khabar) is: ﴿as if they had never dwelt therein﴾ — they had not stayed there. (Ghaniya bi-l-makan: he remained/resided in the place.)

﴿Those who denied Shu'ayb﴾ is a subject (mubtada'), whose predicate is: ﴿they were the losers﴾ — not those to whom they said: ﴿Indeed, you would then be losers﴾. In this beginning (ibtida') there is the meaning of exclusivity (ikhtisas), as if it were said: those who denied Shu'ayb are those singled out to be destroyed, as if they had never resided in their homes, because those who followed Shu'ayb were saved by Allah. Those who denied Shu'ayb are those singled out for the great loss, unlike those who followed him, so they are the winners. In this repetition there is emphasis and a magnification of their denial and of what befell them.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 93:

﴿Then he turned away from them﴾ after the punishment had descended upon them. ﴿And he said: "O my people, I had certainly conveyed to you the messages of my Lord and advised you sincerely, so how should I grieve over a disbelieving people?"﴾ He (Shu'ayb, peace be upon him) grieved intensely over his people. Then he rebuked himself and said: How could my grief be so intense over a people who are not deserving of grief over them, because of their disbelief and their deserving what has descended upon them?! Or he meant: I had certainly given you every excuse in conveying and warning you about what would befall you, but you did not believe me, so how should I grieve over you?!

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 94:

﴿And We did not send a prophet to any town without afflicting its people with adversity and hardship, so that they might humble themselves.﴾ It is said: every city is a "qarya" (town), and there is an ellipsis here, meaning: so they denied him. ﴿Except that We seized its people with distress﴾, i.e., with misery and poverty, ﴿and hardship﴾, i.e., harm and sickness, because of their arrogance in refusing to follow their prophet. Or the two terms refer to loss of life and property.

﴿So that they might humble themselves﴾: the phrase "yaddarra'una" (لَعَلَّهم يَضَّرَّعُونَ) means "li-yatadarra'u" (so that they might supplicate humbly), "wa-yatadhallalu" (and abase themselves), and "wa-yahuttu" (and lay down) "ardiyat al-kibr" (the cloaks of pride).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 95:

﴿Then We replaced the evil with good﴾ i.e., We gave them, in place of the hardship and affliction they had been in, ease, abundance and health. ﴿Until they multiplied﴾ — they increased and grew in their persons and their wealth, from their saying "ʿafā al-nabāt" (the plant grew abundantly) when it became plentiful. From this is his saying ﷺ: "Let the beards grow (wa-aʿfū al-liḥā)."  ﴿And they said: Surely adversity and prosperity have touched our fathers too﴾ i.e., they said: this is the custom of time, which alternates among people between adversity and prosperity, and such things have touched our fathers as well; it is not a punishment for sin, so remain as you are.

﴿So We seized them suddenly﴾ — unexpectedly, ﴿while they did not perceive﴾ the descent of the punishment.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 96:

The lam in ﴿And if the people of the towns﴾ is a reference to the people of the towns that were indicated by ﴿We did not send any warner to a town﴾. It is as if he said: "And if the people of the towns who denied and were destroyed ﴿had believed﴾ instead of their disbelief, and ﴿had been mindful of God﴾ (ittaqaw), abandoning associating partners in place of committing it, ﴿We would have opened up for them﴾ (la-fattahna, with the doubled ta', is the reading of al-Shami)."

﴿blessings from the heaven and the earth﴾: he means rain and vegetation, or it means that We would have brought them good from every direction. ﴿But they denied﴾ the prophets, ﴿so We seized them for what they had earned﴾ on account of their disbelief and the evil of their earning. It is also permissible that the lam be for the genus (li-l-jins).

﴿Do the people of the towns feel secure﴾, meaning: the disbelievers among them.

﴿that Our punishment, [i.e., Our torment,] will come upon them﴾ ﴿بَياتًا﴾ (at night), [meaning] during the time of the night, as one says: باتَ بَياتًا (he spent the night). ﴿while they are asleep﴾

(p-٥٨٩)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 98:

﴿Or do the people of the towns feel secure that Our punishment will not come upon them by day, while they are at play?﴾ "By day" means in daylight. Ad-duha (the forenoon, the time when the sun has risen and its light is bright) is, in origin, the light of the sun when it has risen. The fa' (فاء) and the waw (واو) in "afa-amina" and "awa-amina" are conjunctions (حرفا عطف, ḥarfā ʿatf) into which the interrogative hamza of denial (همزة الإنكار, hamzat al-inkār) has entered. The element conjoined to ("al-ma'tuf 'alayhi") is ﴿So We seized them suddenly﴾. The statement ﴿And if the people of the towns had believed and feared God...﴾ up to ﴿they used to earn﴾ is a parenthetical insertion (اعتراض, iʿtirāḍ) between the conjoined element and that to which it is conjoined. It was conjoined with fa' because the meaning is: they did, and they acted, so We seized them suddenly. Then: after that, did the people of the towns feel secure that Our punishment would not come upon them by night, or did they feel secure that it would not come upon them by day? (Aw amina) is the reading of Ibn Amir (Shami) and the Hijazi readers, on the basis of coordination with "aw" (أو, "or"). The meaning is the denial of security from either of these two forms of the punishment coming: at night, or in the forenoon. If you say: how did the interrogative hamza enter upon the conjunction particle, when it contradicts the interrogative? I say: the contradiction exists in a single word, not in coordinating one clause with another, because it is on the resumption of one clause after another. ﴿While they are at play﴾ means: they are occupied with what benefits them nothing.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 99:

﴿Afa-amintu﴾ (﴿Do they then feel secure?﴾) is a repetition of His words: ﴿Do the people of the towns feel secure﴾ ﴿from the plan of Allah?﴾ The plan (makr) of Allah is His seizing the servant from where he does not perceive. And it is related from al-Shibli (may Allah sanctify his spirit, the Mighty) that His plan with them is His leaving them as they are. The daughter of al-Rabi' ibn Khuthaym said to her father: "Why do I see people sleeping while you do not sleep?" He said: "My daughter, your father fears the night raid," meaning His words: ﴿that Our punishment comes upon them by night while they are sleeping﴾. ﴿None feels secure from the plan of Allah except the losing people﴾, except the disbelievers, who lost themselves until they came to the Fire.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 100:

﴿Had it not become clear (yuhdi, lit. "make clear, explain")﴾ to ﴿those who inherit the earth after its former inhabitants that, if We willed, We could smite them for their sins﴾? ﴿That if We willed﴾ is in the nominative, being the agent (fa'il) of "yahdi." The "an" here is a lightened form (mukhaffafah) of the heavy "inna" (an-na-mukhaffafah min ath-thaqilah). That is: "Has it not become clear to those who succeed those who passed before them in their dwellings, and who inherit their land, that this is the matter: that if We willed, We could smite them for their sins, just as We smote those before them, so We would destroy the inheritors just as We destroyed the inherited?" The verb of guidance (al-hidayah) has been made transitive with the preposition "li-" (to) because it carries the sense of "tabyin" (making clear).

﴿And We seal﴾ is a resumptive (mustaʼnaf) clause, meaning: "and We set a seal."

﴿upon their hearts, so they do not hear﴾ the admonition.

Al-Nasafi, *Madarik al-Tanzil*, commentary on Surah 7, verse 101:

﴿Those are the cities; We relate to you some of their news.﴾ Like His saying: ﴿And this is my husband, an old man﴾ [Hud: 72], in that it is a *mubtada'* (subject) and *khabar* (predicate) and *hal* (circumstantial clause). Or "al-qura" (the cities) may be a *sifah* (qualifier) of "tilka" (those), and "naqussu" (We relate) is the *khabar*. The meaning is: those cities mentioned, from the people of Nuh (Noah) to the people of Shu'ayb (Shu'ayb), We relate to you some of their news, and they have other news that We have not related to you. ﴿And their messengers certainly came to them with clear proofs﴾, with miracles. ﴿But they were not going to believe﴾ at the coming of the messengers with the clear proofs ﴿in what they had denied before﴾, meaning, in the signs of Allah that they had denied before the coming of the messengers. Or: ﴿they were not going to believe﴾ until the end of their lives in what they had first denied when the messengers came to them. That is, they persisted in denial from the time the messengers came to them until they died, remaining obstinate despite the successive signs. The *lam* in "*li-yu'minu*" (لِيُؤْمِنُوا) is for emphasizing the negation. ﴿Thus﴾, like that strong sealing, ﴿Allah seals the hearts of the disbelievers﴾, since He knew of them that they would choose to remain steadfast in disbelief.

﴿And We did not find for most of them any covenant﴾. The pronoun (ḍamīr) refers to people in general, meaning that most people broke the covenant of God and His pact of faith. The verse is a parenthetical interjection (i'tirāḍ). Alternatively, it refers to the nations mentioned, for when they made a covenant with God in hardship and fear, saying, "If You deliver us, we will surely believe," and then He delivered them, they broke it. ﴿And indeed﴾: the إنْ here is the light (mukhaffafa) form of إنّ, meaning "truly" and "the matter/statement is that." ﴿We found most of them defiantly disobedient﴾, meaning departing from obedience. The verb وجد here means "to know," as shown by the entry of the light إنْ and the distinguishing lām (al-lām al-fāriqa). This is not permissible except with the subject (mubtada'), the predicate (khabar), and the verbs that enter upon them.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 103:

﴿Then We sent after them Moses﴾. The pronoun refers either to the messengers mentioned in His words ﴿And there had certainly come to them their messengers﴾, or to the nations. ﴿With Our signs﴾, meaning with the clear miracles, ﴿to Pharaoh and his chiefs, but they wronged them thereby﴾, meaning they disbelieved in Our signs. He treated wronging (ẓulm) as equivalent to disbelief (kufr), because the two are of one kind, as in His words ﴿Indeed, association [of others with Allah] is a great wrong﴾ [Luqman: 13]. Or the meaning is: they wronged people through them, when they harmed whoever believed. Since belief in them was obligatory, and they disbelieved instead of believing, their disbelief in them was a wrong, since they placed disbelief in a place other than its proper place, which is the place of belief. ﴿So observe how was the end of the corrupters﴾, namely that they became drowned.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 104:

﴿And Moses said, "O Pharaoh!"﴾ It is said of the kings of Egypt: al-Faraʿina (the Pharaohs), just as it is said of the kings of Persia: al-Akasira (the Khosraus). So it is as if he said: "O king of Egypt." His name was Qabus; or al-Walid ibn Mus'ab ibn al-Rayyan.

﴿Indeed, I am a messenger from the Lord of the worlds﴾ to you. Pharaoh said: "You have lied." So Moses said:

Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on Surah 7, verse 105:

﴿It is incumbent upon me that I should not say of God anything but the truth.﴾ That is: I am bound to speak the truth, meaning that it is obligatory upon the one who speaks the truth that he be its speaker and its upholder. (حَقِيقٌ عَلَيَّ) is the reading of Nafi', meaning: it is obligatory upon me to refrain from saying anything about God except the truth, that is, what is true. According to this reading, one pauses at "*al-'Alamin*" (the worlds). According to the first reading, it is permissible to continue without pause, by making *haqiq* a description of the Messenger. "*'Ala*" (عَلى) here carries the meaning of "*ba'*" (الباء), as in the reading of Ubayy (ibn Ka'b). That is: "I am a messenger worthy of not saying anything but the truth." Alternatively, *'ala* may be taken as connected to a verbal sense within "messenger," meaning: "I am a messenger who is deserving and fit for the mission, sent on the condition that I should not say anything about God except the truth."

﴿I have indeed come to you with a clear sign from your Lord.﴾ That is, with what makes my mission clear.

﴿So send with me the Children of Israel.﴾ That is, let them go with me, returning to the Holy Land which is their homeland. The reason for this is that when Yusuf (peace be upon him) died, Pharaoh (Fir'awn) overpowered the descendants of the Tribes (al-Asbat) and enslaved them. God rescued them through Musa (peace be upon him). The period between the day Yusuf (peace be upon him) entered Egypt and the day Musa entered it was four hundred years.

("*ma'i*" (مَعِي) is the reading of Hafs.)

Pharaoh said: ﴿If you have come with a sign﴾ from the One who sent you, ﴿then produce it, if you are among the truthful﴾. Bring it to me, so that your claim may be established and your truthfulness in it may be proven.

(p-592)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 107:

﴿So he cast down⟩ Musa, upon him be peace, ﴿his staff⟩ from his hand, ﴿and behold, it was⟩ "idha" here is for sudden surprise (lil-mufajaʼa), and it is among the adverbs of place, in the position of "thamma" (there), and "hunaka" (there): ﴿a serpent⟩, a great snake, ﴿clearly visible⟩, its matter being evident. It is related that it was a male serpent, gaping its mouth, between its two jaws there were eighty cubits; it placed its lower jaw on the ground and its upper jaw on the wall of the palace. Then it turned towards Pharaoh and he fled, and he defecated, having not defecated before that, and it charged upon the people, and twenty-five thousand of them died, some of them killing others. Pharaoh cried out: "O Musa, take it, and I will believe in you." So Musa took it, and it returned to being a staff.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 108:**

﴿And he drew out his hand﴾ from his bosom, ﴿and behold, it was white to the onlookers﴾. That is: behold, it was white to the spectators (al-nazzara). It would not be white to the spectators unless it were a strange whiteness, outside the ordinary custom, which gathers people to look at it. It is related that he showed Pharaoh his hand, and [Pharaoh] said: "What is this?" [Moses] said: "Your hand." Then he put it back into his bosom and drew it out, and behold, it was white, its radiance overpowering the radiance of the sun. And Moses, peace be upon him, was ādam (dark-complexioned), of intense darkness of complexion.

﴿The chiefs among the people of Pharaoh said, "Indeed, this is a knowing sorcerer."﴾ (He is) knowledgeable in sorcery and skilled in it. He has deceived the people's eyes so that they saw the staff as a serpent and the *al-ādam* (white) [hand] as white.

This statement is attributed to Pharaoh in Surat al-Shu'ara', where he is said to have spoken it to the chiefs (*al-mala'*). Here it is attributed to the chiefs themselves. So it is possible that he said it, and they also said it: the Qur'an relates his statement there and their statement here. Or he said it at the outset, and the chiefs took it from him (*talaqqanahu*), so they repeated it to their *a'qāb* (successors/followers).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 110:

﴿He wants to drive you out of your land﴾, meaning: Egypt. ﴿So what do you advise?﴾, i.e., what do you suggest? From āmartuhu (I consulted him), as in: "I consulted him (ātamartuhu), so he advised me (fa-amarani) to do such-and-such," when you consult someone and he gives you an opinion (fa-ashāra ʿalayka bi-ra'y). This is part of the speech of Pharaoh, who said it to the chiefs (al-mala') when they said to him: ﴿Indeed, this is a knowing sorcerer﴾ ﴿He wants to drive you out of your land﴾

(p-593)

111 (﴿قالُوا أرْجِهْ﴾) With the ha pronounced with sukun (أرْجِهْ): ʿĀṣim and Ḥamzah. It means: postpone and detain him, that is, delay his affair and do not hasten. Or it is as if he (Pharaoh) had intended to kill him, so they said: postpone his killing, detain him, and do not kill him, so that his sorcery may be made evident before the people. ﴿وَأخاهُ﴾ (and his brother) Hārūn. ﴿وَأرْسِلْ في المَدائِنِ حاشِرِينَ﴾ (and send into the cities gatherers), meaning those who assemble.
﴿They will bring you every skilled sorcerer﴾. (Sahhar) is the reading of Hamzah and ʿAli, meaning: they will bring you every skilled sorcerer like him in proficiency, or better than him.

And the sorcerers came to Pharaoh, meaning: he sent for them and they came. ﴿They said: Indeed for us there is surely a reward,﴾ stated as a report and affirming a great reward. This is the reading of Hijazi (the reading of the Hijaz) and Hafs. He did not say "fa-qalu" (then they said), because it is as if a questioner had asked: "What did they say when they came to him?" So it was answered with his words: ﴿They said: Indeed for us there is surely a reward﴾, a wage (ju'l) in case of victory. The indefiniteness of "ajran" is for magnification, as if they had said: "We must have a great reward," ﴿if we are indeed the victors.﴾

"He said: 'Yes indeed; and you will be among those brought near [to me].'" (Qur'an 7:114)

Here the Qur'anic words are rendered as: ﴿He said, "Yes"﴾ — that there is indeed a reward for you, and ﴿you will indeed be among those brought near﴾ to me. Thus you will be the first to enter and the last to leave. They were eighty thousand, or seventy thousand, or some thirty-odd thousand.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 115:

﴿They said: "O Musa, either you throw, or we become the throwers."﴾ [your staff] ﴿and either we become the throwers﴾ [what is with us]. In it there is an indication that their desire was to throw first, since they emphasized their attached pronoun with a detached one (nahnu) and made the predicate definite (al-mulqin).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 116:

﴿Said﴾ Musa (peace be upon him) to them: ﴿Throw﴾. Their giving him the choice is good manners, which they observed with him, as debaters do before they plunge into dispute. Musa permitted them what they desired, out of contempt for their affair, indifference toward them, and reliance on the fact that a miracle will never be overcome by magic ever.

﴿Throw.﴾ ﴿So when they threw, they bewitched the eyes of the people﴾, deceiving them through tricks (hiyal) and sleight of hand (sha'wadha), and imagining to them what the reality was contrary to. It is related that they threw thick ropes and long staves, and behold, they were like serpents that filled the earth, and some of them mounted others. ﴿And they terrified them﴾, frightening them with a severe fright, as if they had sought their dread through trickery. ﴿And they brought forth a great magic﴾, in the domain of magic, or in the eyes of whoever saw it.

And We revealed to Moses: "Throw down your staff," and behold, it swallowed up what they had falsified. "Talqafu": it swallows. (Talqaf) is read by Hafs with the sukun on the fa'. ﴿مَا يَأْفِكُونَ﴾ "Ma" is either a relative pronoun (mawsulah) or a verbal-noun particle (masdariyyah). The meaning is: what they falsify (ya'fikunahu), i.e., they turn it away from the truth to falsehood and fabricate it; or "ifkuhum" is a designation of the thing falsified by the term "ifk" (falsehood). It is narrated that when it swallowed up the whole valley's worth of wood and ropes, Moses picked it up, and it returned to being a staff as it was. God, by His power, annihilated those enormous bodies, or broke them into very fine particles. The sorcerers said: "If this were sorcery, our ropes and our staffs would have remained."
﴿So the truth came to pass﴾: it occurred and was established, ﴿and what they had been doing was nullified﴾ of the magic.

**﴿So they were overcome there﴾**, that is: Pharaoh, his troops, and the magicians.

**﴿and they returned humbled﴾**, and they became abased and bewildered.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 120:

﴿And the sorcerers were thrown down, prostrating.﴾ They fell prostrate to Allah, as if someone had thrown them down because of the intensity of their falling, or because they could not restrain themselves from what they had seen; so it was as if they had been cast down. They were, at the beginning of the day, disbelieving sorcerers, and at its end, righteous martyrs.

﴿They said: "We believe in the Lord of the worlds, ﴾ ﴿the Lord of Moses and Aaron."﴾ This is a *badal* (a substitute, in grammatical terms, a word that replaces and restates the one before it) for what precedes it.

﴿They said: "We believe in the Lord of the worlds, ﴾ ﴿the Lord of Moses and Aaron."﴾ This is a *badal* (a substitute, in grammatical terms, a word that replaces and restates the one before it) for what precedes it.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 123:

﴿Pharaoh said: "Do you believe in him before I have given you permission? Indeed, this is a scheme you have devised in the city, to drive its people out of it. But you will come to know."﴾

123 (﴿Pharaoh said: "Do you believe in him..."﴾) Read as a declarative statement by Ḥafṣ. This is a rebuke from him to them. Read by the Kufans other than Ḥafṣ with two hamzas, in which case the first is the hamzat al-istifham (the interrogative hamza), and its meaning is denial and disapproval. ﴿before I have given you permission﴾ means: before my permission to you.

﴿Indeed, this is a scheme you have devised in the city (p-595) to drive its people out of it﴾ Indeed, your action is a stratagem that you and Musa have contrived in Egypt, before you went out into the desert, for a purpose of your own, namely to drive the Copts out of Egypt and have the Children of Israel settle in their place. ﴿But you will come to know﴾ is a threat, which he stated in summary and then explained in detail with his words:

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 124:

﴿Surely I will cut off your hands and your feet on opposite sides﴾, [meaning] from every side, a limb; ﴿then I will crucify you all﴾. He was the first to cut off [limbs] on opposite sides, and to crucify.

They said, "Indeed, to our Lord we are returning." ﴿Indeed, to our Lord we are returning.﴾ So we do not care about death, since our turning back is to meeting our Lord and His mercy. Or [it means]: indeed, all of us, meaning themselves and Pharaoh, will turn back to God, and He will judge between us.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 126:

﴿And you resent us for nothing except that we believed in the signs of our Lord when they came to us﴾. Wa-ma ta'ību minnā illā al-īmāna bi-āyāti Allāh (you find no fault in us except belief in the signs of God). They meant: you find no fault in us except what is the root of virtues and glories, and that is belief (īmān). From this is his saying:

Poetry:
"There is no fault in them, except that their swords
are, by them, notched from the clashing of battalions."

﴿Our Lord, pour upon us patience﴾, i.e., pour it out abundantly (aṣubb ṣabban dhari'an). The meaning is: grant us abundant patience, and increase it upon us until it overflows us and covers us, just as water is poured out in a flood. ﴿And cause us to die as Muslims﴾, firm upon Islam.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 127:

﴿And the chiefs of the people of Pharaoh said: "Will you leave Musa and his people to spread corruption in the land?"﴾ (the land of Egypt) by exalting themselves in it and changing the religion of its people, for he (Musa) had agreed with the magicians on faith, six hundred thousand men. ﴿And leave you and your gods?﴾ is coordinated (ʿatf) with "to spread corruption" (liyufsidu). It is said: Pharaoh made idols for his people and commanded them to worship them as a means of drawing near to him, just as the worshippers of idols worship, and they would say: (p-596) "They bring us near to God in closeness." For this reason he said: ﴿I am your lord, the Most High﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 24]. ﴿He said﴾ — Pharaoh, responding to the chiefs — ﴿"We will kill their sons and spare their women, and indeed we are dominant over them."﴾ (sanaqtulu) is the reading of the Hijazi (reciters), meaning: we will renew the killing of the sons against them, so that they know that we are still in the same state of dominance and subjugation as we were, and that they are subdued under our hands as they were, and so that the common people do not imagine that he is the boy about whom the astrologers spoke, that our kingdom would end at his hand, which would then discourage them from obeying us and call them to follow him.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 128:

﴿Musa said to his people: "Seek help from Allah and be patient."﴾ He said this to them when they became distressed by the words of Pharaoh: ﴿"We will kill their sons"﴾, as consolation for them and as a promise of victory over them.

﴿Indeed, the earth﴾: the definite article (al-lam) is for previous reference (ʿahd), meaning the land of Egypt; or it is for the generic class (jins), in which case it encompasses the land of Egypt in a primary sense.

﴿belongs to Allah. He causes whomever He wills of His servants to inherit it﴾: in this is his (Musa's) expectation for them of the land of Egypt. ﴿And the good outcome is for the God-conscious (al-muttaqun)﴾: a glad tidings that the praiseworthy end belongs to the God-conscious among them and among the Copts. This sentence is free of the conjunction waw, because it is a resumptive sentence (jumla mustaʾnafa), unlike His saying: ﴿And the chiefs of the people of Pharaoh said﴾, because it is conjoined (maʿtuffa) to what preceded it from His saying: ﴿The chiefs of the people of Pharaoh said﴾.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 129:**

﴿They said: "We were harmed before you came to us and after you came to us."﴾ They mean: the killing of their sons before the birth of Musa (Moses), until he was made a prophet, and its renewal against them after that. This is a complaint about Fir'awn (Pharaoh) and an expression of impatience for the promise of victory.

﴿He said: "It may be that your Lord will destroy your enemy and make you successors in the land."﴾ This is an explicit statement of the good news that Allah had earlier conveyed in symbolic form, and He revealed it. It is the destruction of Fir'awn and their succession to his position in the land of Egypt after him.

﴿So that He may see how you act.﴾ That He may see what is done by you, of good and bad deeds, and of gratitude for blessings and ingratitude for them, in order to reward you according to what is found in you. It is related on the authority of Amr ibn Ubayd that he entered upon al-Mansur before the caliphate, and there was on his table one loaf or two loaves. Al-Mansur asked for more for Amr, but none was found. So Amr recited this verse. Then he entered upon him after he had become caliph, and mentioned that to him. (p-٥٩٧) He said: "There remains ﴿so that He may see how you act﴾."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 130:

﴿And We certainly seized the people of Pharaoh with years [of drought]﴾: the years of dearth, and they were seven years. The word "sanah" (year) is among the names that have become dominant, like "dabbah" (beast) and "najm" (star), [meaning it has come to denote a particular thing by general usage].

﴿and a loss of fruits﴾: it has been said that the years of drought were for the people of the desert, and the loss of fruits for the cities. ﴿So that they might be mindful﴾: so that they would take heed and be admonished. They were thereby alerted that this [affliction] was due to their persistence in disbelief, and because people in a state of hardship are more humble in their cheeks and softer in their hearts. It has also been said: Pharaoh lived four hundred years, during which he did not see any hardship for three hundred and twenty years; and had a pain, or hunger, or fever afflicted him during that period, he would not have claimed lordship.

﴿فَإذا جاءَتْهُمُ الحَسَنَةُ﴾ [When good came to them]: health and fertility (al-khisb). ﴿قالُوا لَنا هَذِهِ﴾ [they said, "This is ours"], i.e., this is what we deserve. ﴿وَإنْ تُصِبْهم سَيِّئَةٌ﴾ [And if an evil befell them]: drought (jadb) and sickness.

﴿يَطَّيَّرُوا﴾ [yaṭṭayyarū] Its original form is yatatayyarū, and the tā' was assimilated (idgham) into the ṭā', because both are articulated from the tip of the tongue and the roots of the upper front teeth. ﴿بِمُوسى ومَن مَعَهُ﴾ [with Mūsā and those with him]: they regarded them as a bad omen (tashā'amū bihim), and said, "This is because of their ill omen. Were it not for them, it would not have befallen us." The particle "إذا" [idhā] was used with the good (al-ḥasanah), and the good was made definite; the particle "إنْ" [in] was used with the evil (al-sayyi'ah), and the evil was made indefinite. This is because the category of good occurs as if it were existent, due to its frequency, whereas evil occurs only rarely, and only some of it occurs.

﴿ألا إنَّما طائِرُهُمْ﴾ [Behold, their omen is only] the cause of their good and their evil, ﴿عِنْدَ اللهِ﴾ [with God]: in His judgment and His will. God is the One who decrees what befalls them of good and evil. ﴿قُلْ كُلٌّ مِن عِنْدِ اللهِ﴾ [Say, "All is from God"] [An-Nisa: 78]. ﴿وَلَكِنَّ أكْثَرَهم لا يَعْلَمُونَ﴾ [But most of them do not know] this.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 132:

﴿And they said, "Whatever sign you bring us to bewitch us with, we will not believe you."﴾ The original form of "mahma" is "mama," where the first "ma" is for conditionality (jaza'), and to it is joined the second "ma," which is an added (mazidah) particle that emphasizes the conditional meaning, as in your saying: "Matä ma takhruj akhruj" (whenever you go out, I will go out).

﴿Wherever you may be﴾ [al-Baqarah: 148] and ﴿And if We take you away﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 41]. Except that the alif was changed into a hā' (ha) to avoid the repetition of two similar sounds (istithqalan li-takrir al-mutajanisayn). This is the sound (sadid) view of the Basran school (al-madhhab al-sadid al-Basri), and it is in the accusative position (fi mawdi' al-nasb) governed by "ta'tina" (you bring us), meaning: "Whatever thing you bring us [i.e., you bring us] by it..." And ﴿of a sign﴾ is an explanation (tabyin) of "mahma." The pronoun in "bihi" (with it) and "biha" (with it) refers back to "mahma"; however, the first was made masculine according to the wording (al-lafz), and the second was made feminine according to the meaning (al-ma'na), because it carries the meaning of "ayah" (sign). They called it a sign only in consideration of how Musa was named (i'tibaran li-tasmiyat Musa), or they intended thereby mockery (al-istihza').

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 133:**

﴿So We sent upon them the flood﴾: that which overwhelmed them (ṭāfa bihim), and overcame them, from rain or a torrent. It is said: the water rose above their tilled land. They were rained upon for eight days in intense darkness, not seeing sun or moon, and no one could leave his house. It is also said: the water entered the houses of the Copts (al-Qibṭ) until they stood in the water up to their collarbones, so whoever sat down drowned, while not a drop of the water entered the houses of the Children of Israel. Or it was the smallpox (al-judarī), or the plague (al-ṭāʿūn).

﴿and the locusts﴾: they ate their crops, their fruits, the roofs of their houses, and their clothing, and none of it entered the houses of the Children of Israel.

﴿and the lice﴾: which are the dabā (young locusts before their wings grow), or fleas, or large ticks (qirādān).

﴿and the frogs﴾: they would fall into their food and drink, so that when a man spoke, a frog would fall into his mouth.

﴿and the blood﴾: that is, nosebleeds. It is also said: their water turned into blood, so that when a Copt and an Israelite gathered around one vessel, the side nearest the Israelite was water and the side nearest the Copt was blood. It is also said: the Nile flowed over them as blood.

﴿signs﴾: a state of the things mentioned.

﴿detailed﴾: clarified and manifest, such that no intelligent person could be confused that they are signs of God. Or: separated, with a month between each two signs.

﴿But they were arrogant﴾ toward believing in Moses, ﴿and they were a criminal people﴾.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 134:

﴿When the punishment (ar-rijz) befell them﴾: the final punishment, which was the blood (ad-dam), or the punishments mentioned, one after another. ﴿They said: "O Musa, call upon your Lord for us by virtue of what He has covenanted with you"﴾. "Ma" is a verbal-noun particle (masdariyyah), meaning: by His covenant with you, which is prophethood. The "ba" (bi) is connected to "ud'u" (call upon), meaning: call upon God for us, seeking intercession through Him by His covenant with you (p-599) ﴿"If you remove the punishment from us, we will surely believe in you, and we will surely send the Children of Israel with you"﴾.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 135:

﴿So when We removed from them the punishment until a term﴾, up to a limit of time, ﴿which they were to reach﴾, without doubt. Then they would be punished in it, and the respite granted to them earlier and the removal of the punishment up to its descent would not benefit them.

﴿Then, behold, they broke their word﴾. The answer to "lamma" (when) is "idha" (behold), meaning: when We removed the punishment from them, they suddenly broke their word and did not delay it.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 136:

﴿So We took retribution from them﴾ is the opposite of favour (inʿam), just as punishment (ʿiqab) is the opposite of reward (thawab). ﴿So We drowned them in the sea (al-yamm)﴾: it is the sea whose depth cannot be reached, or it is the deep surging part of the sea and most of its water. Its derivation is from tayammum (intending), because those who benefit from it head towards it,

﴿because they denied Our signs and were heedless of them﴾: meaning, their drowning was due to their denying the signs and their heedlessness of them, and their scant reflection upon them.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 137:

﴿And We made the people who had been oppressed inherit the eastern and western parts of the land, which We had blessed.﴾ They are the Children of Israel, whom Pharaoh and his people oppressed by killing and by enslavement. ﴿The eastern and western parts of the land﴾ means the land of Egypt and the Levant (al-Sham). ﴿Which We had blessed﴾ with fertility, abundance of provision, and many rivers and trees. ﴿And the good word of your Lord was fulfilled for the Children of Israel﴾: this refers to His saying, ﴿Perhaps your Lord will destroy your enemy and make you successors in the land﴾ [Al-A'raf: 129], or to His saying, ﴿And We wished to show favour to those who were oppressed in the land and to make them leaders and to make them the inheritors﴾ up to ﴿what they had been fearing﴾ [Al-Qasas: 5-6]. "Al-ḥusnā" is the feminine of "al-aḥsan" and is an attribute of "al-kalima" (the word). "ʿAlā" is the complement (ṣila) of "tammat", meaning that it continued over them and persisted, from your saying tamma ʿalā al-amr, when he persisted in the matter. ﴿Because they were patient﴾: because of their patience. Consider how this urges patience, and indicates that whoever meets affliction with despair, God leaves him to it, while whoever meets it with patience, God guarantees him relief. (p-600) ﴿And We destroyed﴾: We annihilated,

﴿what Pharaoh and his people had been building﴾ of structures and the construction of palaces.

﴿and what they had been erecting﴾ of gardens, or what they had been raising of lofty buildings toward the sky, such as the tower of Haman and others. With a ḍamma on the rāʾ (yaʿrushūna): Shāmī and Abū Bakr.

This is the end of the story of Pharaoh and the Copts, and of their denial of God's signs. Then He followed it with the story of the Children of Israel, and what they introduced after their deliverance from Pharaoh, their witnessing of the great signs, and their crossing of the sea, namely the worship of the calf and other things, in order to console the Messenger of God (ﷺ) for what he saw from the Children of Israel in Medina.

﴿And We brought the Children of Israel across the sea﴾. It is related that Moses led them across on the Day of ʿĀshūrāʾ (the tenth of Muharram), after Allah had destroyed Pharaoh and his people, and so they fasted it in gratitude to Allah. ﴿Then they came upon a people﴾, so they passed by them, ﴿who were devoted to worshipping their idols﴾, persisting in their worship of them. These were images of a calf. With the vowel of the *kāf* (ﷺ) read as *kasr* (i.e., ﴿yaʿkifūna﴾ with a kasra on the kāf), it is read by Ḥamzah and ʿAlī.

﴿They said: "O Moses, make for us a god"﴾, an idol to which we may devote ourselves, ﴿just as they have gods﴾, idols to which they devote themselves. The word *"mā"* (ما) here is the *kāffa* (the particle that "restrains" the governing force of the verb, here the *kāf* of comparison), and for this reason a full sentence follows it. A Jew said to ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him: "You differed after your Prophet before his water had dried up." He replied: "You said, 'Make for us a god,' and your feet had not yet dried."

﴿He said: "Indeed, you are a people who act in ignorance"﴾. This is an expression of astonishment at their words, coming immediately after they had seen the great sign. So he described them with absolute ignorance and emphasized it.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 139:

﴿Indeed, these﴾ means: the worshippers of those images, ﴿will be destroyed﴾, ruined, from tabar (destruction): ﴿what they are engaged in﴾, meaning: Allah will destroy and demolish the religion they follow at the hands of me. In placing "these" as the subject of inna, and in placing the predicate of the subject before the predicate of the sentence that serves as its predicate, there is a marking of the worshippers of idols as those exposed to destruction, and that it will not by any means pass them by. ﴿And what they used to do is void﴾, meaning: what they did of worshipping idols is void and perishing.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 140:

﴿Said he: "Shall I seek for you a god other than Allah, when He has preferred you over the worlds?"﴾ That is: "Shall I seek for you a god other than the One deserving of worship? (p-601)" ﴿And He has preferred you over the worlds﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: over the worlds of your own time.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 141:

﴿And when We delivered you from the people of Pharaoh﴾ (anjakum) is the reading of Ibn ʿAmir (al-Shami).

﴿who inflicted on you the worst torment﴾: yabghūnakum shiddat al-ʿadhab (they sought to inflict on you severe torment), from sāma al-silʿata (he sought the commodity), meaning when he seeks it. It is a resumptive clause (istiʾnaf) with no place in i'rab, or it is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring to the addressees, or to the people of Pharaoh.

﴿They slaughtered your sons and spared your women﴾ (yaqtulūna) is the reading of Nafiʿ.

﴿And in that﴾: i.e., in the deliverance, or in the torment.

﴿was a great trial﴾: a blessing (niʿmah), or an affliction (miḥnah) ﴿from your Lord﴾, ʿaẓīm.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 142:**

﴿And We appointed for Musa thirty nights﴾ for the giving of the Torah, ﴿and We completed them with ten﴾. It is narrated that Musa, peace be upon him, had promised the Children of Israel, while he was in Egypt (Misr), that if Allah destroyed their enemy he would bring them a Book from Allah. When Pharaoh (Fir'awn) was destroyed, Musa asked his Lord for the Book, and He commanded him to fast thirty days, which was the month of Dhu al-Qa'dah. When he completed the thirty, he noticed a change in the smell of his mouth (khulūf, the odour of a fasting person's mouth), so he used the siwak (tooth-stick). Allah revealed to him: "Do you not know that the odour of the mouth of one who fasts is more pleasing to Me than the scent of musk?" So He commanded him to add ten days to it from Dhu al-Hijjah, for that reason. ﴿So the appointed time of his Lord was completed﴾, meaning the time that was set for him and fixed for him.

﴿forty nights﴾: the word ʾarbaʿīna laylatan (forty nights) is in the accusative (nuṣiba) as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl), meaning: the appointed time was completed while being exactly this number. The mention of the forty was summarised in al-Baqarah and is detailed here.

﴿And Musa said to his brother Harun﴾: the word Hārūn is in apposition (ʿaṭf bayān, explicative apposition) to "his brother".

﴿Take my place among my people﴾: be my successor (khalīfah) among them.

﴿And act righteously﴾: in what must be set right of the affairs of the Children of Israel. ﴿And do not follow the way of the corrupters﴾: and whoever among them calls you to corruption, do not follow him and do not obey him.

[p. 602] ﴿And when Musa came at Our appointed time﴾ at the time We had appointed for him and set. The meaning of the lam (in *li-miqatina*) is exclusivity (*ikhtisas*), i.e., his coming was specifically at Our appointed time. ﴿And his Lord spoke to him﴾ without an intermediary and without a modality. It is related that he heard the speech from every direction. Shaykh Abu Mansur mentioned in *al-Ta'wilat* that Musa, peace be upon him, heard a sound that indicated the speech of God, the Exalted. His distinction lay in the fact that He made him hear a sound whose creation He Himself undertook, not one acquired by any created being, whereas others hear a sound acquired by servants and understand from it the speech of God, the Exalted. When he heard His speech, he longed to see Him, because his longing overwhelmed him, so he asked for the vision with his words: ﴿He said, "My Lord, show me [Yourself] that I may look at You."﴾ The second object of *arini* ("show me") is omitted, meaning: "Show me Your Essence that I may look at You," i.e., enable me to see You by manifesting Yourself to me so that I may see You. *(Arini)* is read by Makki with a full vowel on the *ra'*, and with a short vowel on the *ra'* (*mukhtalasa*) by Abu 'Amr, and with a full long vowel (*mushbaʿa*) by the others. This is evidence for Ahl al-Sunnah (the People of the Sunnah) that the vision is possible, for Musa, peace be upon him, believed that God, the Exalted, can be seen, so he asked. And believing that something impossible for God is permissible is disbelief. ﴿He said, "You will not see Me."﴾ [That is] by asking with a perishable eye, but rather by bestowal and grace with an enduring eye. This too is evidence for us, for He did not say, "I will not be seen," which would have been a denial of possibility. And had He not been seen, He would have informed him that He is not seen, since the situation called for clarification. ﴿But look at the mountain; if it remains in its place﴾ and stays in its state ﴿then you will see Me﴾. This too is evidence for us, for He made the vision conditional upon the mountain's remaining stable, and that is possible; and making something contingent upon what is possible indicates its possibility, just as making something contingent upon what is impossible indicates its impossibility. The proof that it is possible is His saying: ﴿He made it crumble to dust﴾, and He did not say "it crumbled" (*indakka*). What God, the Exalted, brought into existence was permissible not to exist had He not brought it into existence, because He is free in His action, and because He, the Exalted, did not despair him of that, nor rebuke him for it. Had it been impossible, He would have rebuked him, as He rebuked Nuh, peace be upon him, saying: ﴿"Indeed, I admonish you lest you be among the ignorant"﴾ [Hud: 46], when he asked for his son to be saved from drowning. ﴿So when his Lord manifested Himself to the mountain﴾ i.e., appeared, and became manifest, manifest without modality. Shaykh Abu Mansur, may God have mercy on him, said: The meaning of "manifested to the mountain" is what al-Ash'ari said: that God, the Exalted, created in the mountain life, knowledge, and sight, until it saw its Lord. This is explicit in establishing that He is visible.

By these points the ignorance of those who deny the vision becomes clear, and their claim that Musa, peace be upon him, knew that he could not see [God], but his people asked him to show them their Lord, as God, the Exalted, related about them with His words: ﴿"We will never believe you until we see God openly"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 55], so he asked for the vision in order that God, the Exalted, might make clear that He is not visible, is false. For if it were as they claimed, he would have said, "Show them that they may look at You," and then said to Him, "They will not see You," because if it were not permissible, Musa, peace be upon him, would not have delayed his response to them, but would have answered them the moment their words reached his ears, for there would be in it an endorsement of disbelief. He, peace be upon him, was sent to change [such beliefs], not to confirm them. Do you not see that when they said to him: ﴿"Make for us a god just as they have gods"﴾, he did not give them respite, but responded to them at once with His words: ﴿"Indeed, you are a people who are ignorant"﴾? ﴿He made it crumble to dust﴾ i.e., made into dust. *Mad-kukan* is a verbal noun in the sense of the passive participle, like *darb al-amir* (the striking of the commander). *Al-daqq* and *al-dakk* are two near-synonymous roots. *(Dakka')* is read by Hamza and 'Ali, meaning level with the ground, with no hillock in it. A she-camel that is *dakka'* is one with no hump. ﴿And Musa fell down unconscious﴾: this is a circumstantial clause (*hal*), meaning he fell down in a swoon. ﴿Then when he regained consciousness﴾ from his swoon, ﴿he said, "Exalted are You! I have repented to You"﴾ from asking [for vision] in this world, ﴿and I am the first of the believers﴾ in Your greatness and majesty, and that You do not grant the vision in this world, although it is possible.

Al-Ka'bi and al-Asamm said: the meaning of His words ﴿"Show me [Yourself] that I may look at You"﴾ is: "Show me a sign by which I will know You by necessity, as if I were looking at You,"

﴿"You will not see Me"﴾: you will not be able to know Me in this attribute,

﴿"But look at the mountain; [if it remains in its place] then you will see Me"﴾: for I will manifest a sign to it. If the mountain remains firm at its manifestation and stays in its place, then you will remain firm for it and be able to bear it. This is corrupt, because He said: ﴿"Show me [Yourself] that I may look at You"﴾ and did not say, "Look at it," and He said: ﴿"You will not see Me"﴾ and did not say, "You will not see My sign." And how can its meaning be: "You will not see My sign," when He had already shown him the greatest of signs, by making the mountain crumble to dust?!

﴿He said, "O Musa, I have chosen you above the people﴾ (I have preferred you over the people of your time) ﴿by My messages﴾, which are the books of the Tawrat (the Torah). (bi-risalati) is a reading attributed to the Hijaz (Hijazi).

﴿and by My speaking﴾, meaning by My speaking to you directly. ﴿So take what I have given you﴾, meaning what I have bestowed on you of the honour of prophethood and wisdom, ﴿and be among the grateful﴾ for the blessing in that, for it is among the greatest of blessings."

It has been said: Musa fell down unconscious on the Day of Arafah, and he was given the Tawrat on the Day of Sacrifice (al-Nahr). Since Harun was a minister (wazir) and a follower of Musa, the choosing (al-istifa') was specific to Musa, peace be upon him.

(p. 604)

And We wrote for him on the tablets. Al-Alwah (the tablets): the Torah, plural of lawh (tablet). They were ten tablets; it is also said seven. They were of emerald; it is also said of wood. They descended from the heavens, and the Torah was upon them. ﴿Of everything﴾ is in the accusative position, as the object of "We wrote."

﴿An admonition and a detailed explanation of everything﴾: this is a substitute (badal) for it. The meaning is: We wrote for him everything that the Children of Israel needed in their religion, of admonitions and detailed explanations of the rulings. It is also said: the Torah that was sent down was seventy camel-loads, and none read all of it except four men: Musa (Moses), Yusha' (Joshua), 'Uzayr (Ezra), and 'Isa (Jesus).

﴿So take it﴾: We said to him, "Take it," coordinated (ʿatf) with "We wrote." The pronoun refers to the tablets, or to "a thing," because it carries the meaning of "things." ﴿With strength﴾: with earnestness and resolve, like the conduct of the Messengers of firm resolve (Ulu al-'Azm).

﴿And enjoin your people to take the best of it﴾: that is, within it are what is good and what is better, such as retaliation (qisas), pardon, self-defense, and patience. So they should take that which is more inclusive of goodness and greater in reward, as in His saying: ﴿And follow the best of what has been sent down to you from your Lord﴾ [Az-Zumar: 55]. ﴿I will show you the abode of the defiantly disobedient﴾: the abode of Pharaoh and his people, which is Egypt, and the dwellings of 'Ad and Thamud, and the destroyed generations, how they were left desolate of them, so that you may take heed and not commit sin like their sin, lest there befall you a punishment like their punishment; or it is Hell.

﴿I will turn away from My signs﴾ from understanding them. Dhu al-Nun, may God sanctify his spirit, said: God refuses to honour the hearts of the idle with the hidden wisdom of the Qur'an. ﴿Those who are arrogant﴾ who act haughtily towards creation and disdain to accept the truth. Its reality is the pretence of greatness, which belongs exclusively to the Creator, may His power be exalted. ﴿in the earth without right﴾ This is a circumstantial phrase (ḥāl), meaning that they are arrogant while not being entitled to it, because arrogance rightfully belongs to God alone. ﴿And if they see every sign﴾ of the signs sent down to them ﴿they will not believe in it. And if they see the way of guidance﴾ the path of the right course of action and the path of guidance. Al-Rushd (the Rushd) is read by Hamza and Ali, and the two forms are like al-Suqm and al-Saqam (two dialectal variants of one word meaning sickness). ﴿they will not take it as a way. And if they see the way of error﴾ misguidance ﴿they will take it as a way.﴾ The position (maḥall) of ﴿That﴾ is nominative, meaning: that turning away (al-ṣarf) ﴿is because they denied Our signs﴾ due to their denial ﴿and were heedless of them﴾ heedlessness of obstinacy and aversion, not heedlessness of inadvertence and ignorance. (p. 605)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 147:

﴿Those who denied Our signs and the meeting of the Hereafter﴾ is an idafa of the verbal noun to its object, meaning: their meeting the Hereafter, and their witnessing its conditions.

﴿Their deeds have become void﴾ is the predicate of "those who" (alladhina). ﴿Are they recompensed except for what they used to do?﴾ This is a denial of the (true) conditions by denying the sending (of messengers).

﴿The people of Moses took, after him﴾ after his departure to al-Ṭūr (Mount Sinai), ﴿from their ornaments﴾. It is attributed to them even though it was borrowed (ʿawāriyy) in their hands, because attribution (al-iḍāfah) occurs on the slightest connection. In this there is evidence that whoever swears not to enter the house of so-and-so and then enters a house he has borrowed breaks his oath (yahnathu). Moreover, they came to own it after those who were destroyed, just as they came to own their other possessions. In this there is also evidence that seizing the property of unbelievers causes their ownership of it to cease. Yes, the one who took it was al-Sāmirī, but they approved of him, so the action was ascribed to them. Al-ḥulliyy is the plural of ḥallī, which is the term for whatever is adorned with gold and silver. (ḥilliyyihim) is read by Ḥamzah and ʿAlī, for harmonization (li-l-ittibāʿ).

﴿a calf﴾ is the object of ﴿took﴾.

﴿a body﴾ is an apposition to it, meaning a body with flesh and blood like the rest of bodies, ﴿which had a lowing﴾. The lowing is the sound of cows. The second object is omitted, meaning: a god. Then He marvelled at their foolish minds and said: ﴿Did they not see﴾ when they took it as a god ﴿that it does not speak to them, nor guide them to a way?﴾ It is not able to speak, nor to guide to any path, so that they would not choose it over the One who, if the sea were ink for His words, the sea would be exhausted before His words were exhausted. He is the One who guided the creation to the path of truth through the proofs He placed in the intellects and through what He sent down in the Books. (p-606) Then he began and said: ﴿They took it﴾ as a god, so they went ahead with this reprehensible matter, ﴿and they were wrongdoers﴾.

﴿And when they were seized with remorse﴾: when their regret over worshipping the calf intensified. The origin of this is that it is the way of one whose regret intensifies to bite his hand out of grief, so that his hand becomes "fallen into" (maskūṭan fīhā), because his mouth has fallen upon it. "Suqita" (سُقِطَ) is attributed to "fī aydīhim" (فِي أيْدِيهِمْ), and this is of the category of kināyah (metonymy, an indirect expression). Al-Zajjāj (al-Zajjāj) said: its meaning is that remorse fell into their hands, meaning into their hearts and souls, just as one says: "a displeasing matter occurred in his hand," even though it is impossible for it to be in the hand. This is a comparison of what occurs in the heart and the soul to what occurs in the hand and is seen with the eye.

﴿And they saw that they had gone astray﴾: they came to know their error with such clarity that it was as if they had seen it with their own eyes.

﴿They said: "If our Lord does not have mercy on us and forgive us..."﴾ (لَئِنْ لَمْ تَرْحَمْنا رَبَّنا وتَغْفِرْ لَنا): this is the reading of Ḥamzah and ʿAlī, with the second person (taʾ) and "rabbanā" (رَبَّنا) in the accusative. The accusative of "rabbanā" is by way of address (naṣb ʿalā al-nidāʾ).

﴿We shall surely be among the losers﴾: those who are defrauded in this world and in the Hereafter.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on surah 7, verse 150:

﴿When Musa returned﴾ from al-Tur (Mount Sinai) ﴿to his people﴾, the Children of Israel, ﴿angry﴾. This is a *hal* (circumstantial accusative, describing the state of the subject at the time of the action) referring to Musa.

﴿Grieved﴾ is also a *hal*, meaning sorrowful. ﴿He said: "Evil is what you did as my successors after me"﴾, meaning you stood in my place and were my successors.

﴿After me﴾. The address is to the worshippers of the calf, from among the Samiri and his followers, or to Harun and those believers who were with him. This is supported by His saying: ﴿Take my place among my people﴾ [al-A'raf: 142]. The meaning is: ﴿Evil is what you did as my successors﴾, in that you worshipped the calf instead of worshipping God, or in that you did not refrain from worshipping other than God. The subject of *bi'sa* ("evil is") is an implied pronoun, explained by the phrase "what you did as my successors". The object of praise or blame that follows *bi'sa* is omitted; its implied sense is: "Evil is the succession that you did as my successors, your succession." The phrase ﴿after me﴾ means after his statement "you did as my successors", that is, after what they had seen from him of the affirmation of God's oneness and the negation of partners from Him. Or it means after I had been guiding the Children of Israel toward monotheism and restraining them from worshipping the cow, when they said: ﴿Make for us a god just as they have gods﴾ [al-A'raf: 138]. It is incumbent upon successors to follow the conduct of the one who appointed them.

﴿Have you hastened﴾, have you gone ahead ﴿with the command of your Lord﴾, which was: (p-607) my coming to you with the Torah after forty nights. The original sense of *'ajala* (haste) is seeking a thing before its appointed time. It has also been said that *'ajiltum* here means "you abandoned", (with the meaning of "taraktum").

﴿And he threw down the tablets﴾, out of vexation upon hearing the report of the calf, being angry for the sake of God. He was by nature very fierce in anger, while Harun was gentler in disposition, and for this reason he was more beloved to the Children of Israel than Musa. So the tablets shattered, and six-sevenths of them were lifted up, and one-seventh remained. What was lifted up contained the detailed explanation of everything, and what remained contained guidance and mercy.

﴿And he seized his brother by the head﴾, by the hair of his head, in anger at him, because he had not prevented them from worshipping the calf, ﴿dragging him toward himself﴾, in rebuke of him and not in contempt for him. This clause is a *hal* referring to Musa.

﴿He said: "O son of my mother"﴾. The word "son" is built with "mother" on the fatha vowel, like *khamsata 'ashara* (fifteen). With a kasra on the *mim*, it is read by Hamzah, 'Ali, and the Syrian reader (Ibn 'Amir). The original form was *ummi* ("my mother"), and the *ya'* was deleted, being replaced by the kasra. He was the son of his mother and father. He mentioned the mother specifically because she was a believer, and because mentioning her is more likely to evoke compassion.

﴿Indeed, the people deemed me weak and nearly killed me﴾, meaning: I did not neglect to exert effort in restraining them through admonition and warning, but they deemed me weak and resolved to kill me.

﴿So do not let the enemies rejoice at my expense﴾, namely those who worshipped the calf, meaning: do not do to me what would be their wish of demeaning me and harming me.

﴿And do not place me with the wrongdoing people﴾, meaning: do not make me a companion to them through Your anger against me. So when the excuse of his brother became clear to him, he said:

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 151:

﴿He said: "My Lord, forgive me and my brother"﴾ He said this to please his brother and to remove any gloating (shamatah) over him, by including him with himself in the supplication. The meaning is: "Forgive me for what I have neglected regarding my brother's right, and forgive my brother if he was negligent in conducting well the office of succession (khilafah)." ﴿And admit us into Your mercy﴾ meaning Your protection (ʿiṣmah) in this world, and Your Garden (jannah) in the Hereafter. ﴿And You are the Most Merciful of the merciful.﴾

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 152:

﴿Indeed, those who took the calf﴾ as a deity ﴿will be overtaken by anger from their Lord﴾, which is what they were commanded regarding the killing of themselves in repentance,

﴿and humiliation in the life of this world﴾: their expulsion from their homes, for estrangement humbles necks; or the imposition of the jizya (poll tax) upon them. ﴿Thus do We recompense the fabricators﴾, those who lie against Allah. And there is no greater fabrication than the words of the Samiri: ﴿This is your god and the god of Moses﴾ [Ta-Ha: 88].

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 153:

﴿And those who did evil deeds﴾ — that is, of disbelief and sins.

﴿Then repented﴾ — returned to Allah ﴿after them and believed﴾ — and made their faith sincere (akhlasu al-iman). ﴿Indeed, your Lord after them﴾ — i.e., after the evil deeds, or after the repentance — ﴿is Most Forgiving﴾ — One who conceals [their sins] from them, erasing what occurred from them — ﴿Most Merciful﴾ — One who bestows blessing upon them with Paradise. And "inna" with its noun and predicate forms the predicate of "alladhina" (those who). This is a general ruling that encompasses those who took the calf and others. He first magnified their offense, then followed it with the greatness of His mercy, so that it may be known that sins, however great they are, His pardon is greater.

And when the anger of Musa subsided, (because of its intensity, it was as though anger itself was the one commanding Musa to do what he did, so it was said: ﴿And when the anger subsided from Musa﴾). Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is "it calmed down," and it has also been read with this meaning. ﴿He took up the tablets﴾ which he had thrown down, ﴿and in their inscription﴾ and in what was copied from them, that is, what was written. It is on the pattern fu'lah in the sense of maf'ul, like khutbah (sermon, i.e., "that which is delivered"). ﴿Guidance and mercy for those who fear their Lord﴾. The lam entered because the object precedes the verb, and the verb's action toward it is weakened by this consideration.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 155:

﴿And Musa chose from his people﴾ i.e., from among his people; he omitted the preposition (min) and let the verb reach its object directly, ﴿seventy men﴾. It is said: he chose six men from each of the twelve tribes, so they totalled seventy-two men, and he said: "Let two men from among you remain behind." So Kalib (Caleb) and Yusha' (Joshua) stayed behind.

﴿For Our appointed time﴾: to be present for their apology (i'tidar) regarding the worship of the calf.

﴿So when the quake seized them﴾: the violent earthquake (al-zalzalah al-shadidah).

﴿He said: "My Lord, if You had willed, You would have destroyed them before, and me﴾ because of what some of them did of worshipping the calf,

﴿and me﴾ because of my killing of the Coptic man.

﴿Will You destroy us for what the foolish among us did?﴾ i.e., will You destroy us as punishment for what the ignorant among us did, namely the people of the calf?

﴿It is but Your trial﴾: Your testing (ibtila'uk). This refers back to His words: ﴿Indeed, We have tried your people after you﴾ [Ta-Ha: 85]. Musa said: it is that trial of which You informed me, or it is Allah the Exalted's testing of His servants with whatever He wills: ﴿And We test you with evil and good as a trial﴾ [al-Anbiya': 35]. ﴿By it You lead astray﴾ by the trial,

﴿whom You will﴾: those whom You knew would choose misguidance.

﴿And You guide﴾ by it ﴿whom You will﴾: those whom You knew would choose guidance. ﴿You are our Guardian (waliyyuna)﴾: our Master (mawlana), the one who manages our affairs.

﴿So forgive us and have mercy upon us, and You are the Best of the forgivers.﴾

﴿And ordain for us﴾, that is, establish for us, and decree for us, ﴿in this world a good [thing]﴾, meaning well-being, a pleasant life, and success in obedience, ﴿and in the Hereafter﴾, meaning Paradise.

﴿Indeed, we have turned [hudna] to You﴾, meaning we have repented to You. It is said: هادَ إلَيْهِ يَهُودُ (hāda ilayhi yahūdu), when one returns and repents. And al-Hūd (الهُودُ) is the plural of hāʾid (هائِد), who is one who repents.

﴿He said: My punishment﴾ is among His attributes that ﴿I afflict with it whom I will﴾, that is, I do not pardon him.

﴿And My mercy has encompassed all things﴾, that is, among the attributes of My mercy is that it is vast, reaching everything. There is no Muslim or disbeliever except that upon him is the trace of My mercy in this world. ﴿So I will ordain it﴾, that is, this mercy, ﴿for those who fear [ittiqāʾ, i.e., guard against]﴾ shirk (associating partners with God) from among the community of Muhammad (ﷺ), ﴿and give zakat﴾ (the obligatory alms), ﴿and those who believe in Our signs﴾, meaning in all of Our books, ﴿they believe﴾, not disbelieving in any part of them.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 7, verse 157:
